content: The first week of Lil Durk’s murder-for-hire trial featured text messages, an unreleased music video and key testimony from a former member of the Chicago rapper’s Only the Family (OTF) crew. You’re reading Billboard’s weekly Lil Durk trial recap, a one-sheet breakdown of everything that happened in the murder-for-hire case over the past week. Stay tuned here each Friday for all the testimony and big events you might have missed. The trial began Monday (Aug. 24) in Los Angeles federal court, where the “All My Life” hitmaker (Durk Banks) is charged with ordering OTF members to kill rival rapper Quando Rondo in retaliation for the 2020 killing of his close friend and collaborator King Von. Rondo was shot at a Los Angeles gas station in 2022 and survived, but another man known as Lul Pab was killed in the crossfire. During opening statements, prosecutor Daniel Weiner argued that Durk was “consumed with revenge” after Von’s death. Weiner said Durk arranged for numerous OTF associates to travel from Chicago to L.A. and “track, stalk, hunt and kill” Rondo while he waited for updates in a nearby rental house. Two alleged participants in the killing, David “Browneyez” Lindsey and Deandre “OTF Dede” Wilson, are also on trial. Defense lawyer Marissa Goldberg responded in her own opening statement that the rapper had “nothing to do with” the shooting, arguing that there isn’t any evidence showing he paid for a hit on Rondo. Goldberg said the real mastermind of the plot was Kavon “Vonnie” Grant, one of the shooters who has flipped and become a government witness. “He thought, ‘Oh man, I’ve got an insurance policy,’” said Goldberg of Vonnie’s decision to point the finger at Durk. “I’ve got a big fish I can give them.” After openings, the first two days of Durk’s trial focused largely on hard evidence. Surveillance video was played on Tuesday (Aug. 25) from an In-N-Out Burger restaurant, where the shooters allegedly stopped for a bite after killing Pab. A detective who reviewed the tape testified that the men seemed to be “joking around” and “having a good time,” according to Los Angeles Magazine. Also on Tuesday, prosecutors showed numerous text messages sent by Durk after Von’s 2020 death. This included messages where Durk wrote, “I gotta go all out for him,” “I can’t let this slide” and “him dying turning me a different animal.” On Wednesday (Aug. 26), the jurors heard the first of what is expected to be multiple Durk songs admitted as evidence of Durk’s alleged motive. The prosecution played an unreleased 2021 music video for the song “Redman,” which depicts Durk reading news stories about Von’s death and then shooting a man that prosecutors describe as a Rondo “look-alike.” Durk’s lawyers maintain that his music should not be taken literally, but instead ought to be viewed as a performance in which he’s “challenging his emotions through his artwork.” Durk attorney Brian Steel drilled down on this argument while cross-examining an FBI agent about the “Redman” video on Wednesday, per Rolling Stone. “You know that Durk is a musical artist, a poet, true?” Steel asked the agent. The real fireworks began later on Wednesday when the first of multiple cooperating witnesses took the stand: Kacey “OTF Jam” Hester, a Chicago gang member and former friend of Durk’s who has admitted to being one of the shooters who targeted Rondo. According to Courthouse News Service, Jam said during direct testimony on Wednesday and Thursday (Aug. 27) that he regretted participating in the murder of an “innocent” man. He told the jury, “I wasn’t feeling good about it at all. I felt it was sloppy.” Jam testified Thursday that Durk offered a hefty cash reward for the shooting. While this promised sum was never paid, he allegedly received $10,000 to record a track with Durk. After being arrested in 2023 on separate gun charges, he wrote in a note to police, “I know about murders.” “I had to get it off my chest,” said Jam of his decision to become a government informant. “It was weighing on me.” Steel aggressively cross-examined Jam on Thursday and Friday (Aug. 28), pointing out that his story had “dramatically” changed over time. Steel suggested that Jam, who has been in and out of prison for much of his life, is lying about Durk’s involvement because he wants a reduced sentence. “Going home, that’s your mission?” Steel asked the witness, per Rolling Stone. “Me, trying to go home? Yes,” Jam replied. The trial is set to resume Monday and run for several more weeks. It has already drawn some notable spectators, including Ye (formerly Kanye West) and mgk.

"We're just a couple kids from Toronto who started something we believed in. Here we are 20 years later, same kids with bigger dreams. Authentic and VNCE are the perfect partners to help us continue to grow," says Drake. The chart-topping rapper co-founded OVO in 2008 with his close friends and collaborators, entrepreneur Oliver El-Khatib and producer Noah "40" Shebib, originally as a blog and lifestyle movement. The brand went on to become a Canadian staple worldwide, notably through its signature black-and-gold owl logo. It made major expansions into high-end clothing and streetwear. The OVO Sound label also spun off from that brand. In addition to its online store, OVO runs twelve flagship stores across Canada, the U.S. and the U.K., with locations in Toronto, New York and London. The brand has fostered collaborative relationships with some of the world's biggest brands and institutions, curating several high-profile collections in tandem with the likes of MLB, New Era, UFC and the NBA, including an instant-classic merchandise capsule celebrating the Toronto Raptors' 2019 NBA championship title. "OVO has earned a place among the world's most influential lifestyle brands because it has always stood for something authentic and unmistakable," says Jamie Salter, Authentic's founder and executive chairman. "Drake and his team have built something with incredible cultural influence. We see a significant opportunity to take that even further, opening new markets, building new businesses and reaching more people around the world without losing what makes OVO, OVO.” Authentic Brands Group is a major licensing company in the U.S. whose portfolio includes the ownership of major brands like Sports Illustrated magazine, Champion and Nautica, as well as the licensing for the estates of celebrity legends Elvis Presley, Marilyn Monroe and Muhammad Ali. Now, it's taking on one of Canada's biggest brands, whose global success has long been grounded in its hometown of Toronto and the city's essence and culture. Read more here. Canada Stands Firm on CanCon Streaming Regulations Despite Opposition from the U.S. Canada is standing firm when it comes to CanCon. The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) confirmed that it is sticking with its plans to regulate how Canadian content is presented and made available to users on major streaming services, following recent resistance from the United States. A spokesperson from the CRTC tells the Canadian Press it will move forward to determine exactly how streamers must ensure Canadian content is available and visible to audiences and is still finalizing the dates for the regulatory proceedings. The ongoing controversy surrounding the Online Streaming Act, which became law in 2023, reached a fever pitch over the weekend after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. fell through, partly due to the Trump administration's last-minute demand for American streaming platforms to be exempt from Canadian content regulations. "There were some things we wouldn't do. We were not prepared to compromise Canada’s sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Mark Carney said in an extensive speech following the collapse of the discussions. "We were not prepared to compromise on our sovereignty, the protection of the French language, and our culture. To our American colleagues, let us be clear: for my government and for Canada, these issues were never on the table, even though the United States tried until the very last minute." It's the latest development in a continuous back-and-forth between the Canadian government, Canadian companies and U.S. streaming companies, which stems from the controversial Online Streaming Act introduced by the Trudeau government in 2023. In its implementation, the CRTC mandated a 5% tax contribution on all broadcasters making over $25 million, intended to fund the production of Canadian, French language and Indigenous content, which caused major pushback from affected streaming giants like Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon Music. Back in May, the CRTC announced plans to triple that contribution to 15% for audiovisual streaming services like Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Apple TV in an attempt to stabilize the $200 million funding rate for Canadian companies. The Canadian government then stepped in and announced a landmark, $600 million yearly investment, which includes covering the $200 million base contribution that would have otherwise been taxed on foreign streaming services. Beyond financial contributions, discoverability has also been a point of contention during discussions between Canada and the U.S. Back in December, Quebec passed Bill 109, the Act to affirm the cultural sovereignty of Québec, which sought to impose quotas on the amount of French-language content presented and promoted on the homepages of foreign streaming platforms like Netflix and Prime Video. Like with the CRTC, these platforms voiced their displeasure, asking the National Assembly to forego the quotas. Carney stood up for the language's preservation over the weekend, after Trump and his representatives directly denied that the French language was a factor within their talks. "I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Read more here. Juno Awards Restructure Several Categories Ahead of 2027 Ceremony The Juno Awards have announced that they are reshaping certain categories ahead of their 2027 ceremony to more accurately represent current trends in music consumption across Canada, primarily changing certain category names and eligibility criteria. “CARAS is introducing a series of category and eligibility updates designed to better reflect Canada’s music community today and provide clear, meaningful pathways for artists to have their work recognized,” says the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) on the official Junos website. “The changes are informed by CARAS’ annual review of The Juno Awards, working closely with Music Advisory Committees and the broader music community to examine how categories and criteria can continue to serve Canadian artists.” The main changes are mergers or name changes in the rap, reggae/dancehall, electronic/dance and contemporary Christian/gospel music categories. Rap album and EP of the year have now been replaced by melodic rap recording of the year and rap recording of the year, while dance recording of the year and electronic album of the year have been merged under one umbrella (dance/electronic), with respective awards for single/EP of the year and album of the year within the genre. The reggae category has been renamed to reggae/dancehall, reflecting an increasing prevalence of dancehall within the mainstream, given recent hits like MOLIY’s 2025 chart hit, “Shake it to the Max (FLY) - Remix.” The contemporary Christian/gospel album of the year category has also swapped “album” for “recording,” enabling singles and EPs to be included in the running. This year’s awards for "recordings" now accept albums, EPs and singles as submissions, although singles must be standalone releases that do not appear on any short or full-length project. The vocal-instrumental threshold for jazz music has also shifted from 80% to 51%, which speaks to the rise of artists like Laufey and Olivia Dean, whose jazzy style incorporates pop-centric tendencies. The classical music album categories have also shifted to allow compilation albums to be eligible. These changes mark the latest step in the Junos’ ongoing category evolution. Last year, Alex Cuba won the first-ever Latin music recording of the year award, which was introduced amid a blockbuster year for Bad Bunny and his chart-topping album Debí Tirar Más Fotos, which amplified Latin music’s global success on a bigger scale than ever. Before that, the awards introduced the South Asian recording of the year category, which was won this year by Punjabi stars Karan Aujla & Ikky. The Junos have also run into controversy for their category decisions. In 2024, public backlash caused CARAS to backtrack on its decision to axe reggae recording and Christian/gospel album categories — both categories that honour genres led by Black musicians. content: When Dolly Parton was considering selling her music recording and publishing assets back in 2021, she was shopping catalogs which combined had net publishing and net label shares approaching $10 million, say some suitors and other financial sources who were aware of the deal. At the time, the rumor was that her management team was seeking about $500 million; now, other sources suggest discussions were more along the lines of a $230 million valuation. Whatever the price, a deal never closed, and it’s unclear if Parton pulled the deal or a suitor never completed it. The year before that rumor circulated, Parton told Billboard she was contemplating how to put her estate in order. Now, following her passing this week at the age of 80, some wonder if Parton left instructions that her music assets be sold — and if she did, what assets she owned, and what the numbers could be. Related Dolly Parton, One of Country Music's Biggest & Brightest Icons, Dies at 80 Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery How Much Does Her Catalog Generate? Billboard estimates that her master recording catalog and her publishing combined generated $17.5 million in revenue on average over the last four years (2022-2025). But how much of that $17.5 million in revenue she takes home, as well as what is owned assets (known as an active investment) and how much is royalties (known as a passive investment) is less clear. Active music assets are more highly-sought-after than passive music assets, and therefore carry a higher valuation multiple. In 2021, when Parton was testing the waters to sell her music assets, she was coming off the second-biggest year for her catalog in the past decade, according to Luminate data. In 2020, a year largely defined by the COVID pandemic, her catalog generated 764,000 album equivalent units, likely spurred by a new Christmas album, A Holly Dolly Christmas, with an hour-long TV special; high-profile philanthropic work, including a YouTube bedtime story series, “Goodnight With Dolly,” for children; and a Netflix holiday musical film, Christmas On the Square. And the growth in streaming at the time also helped spur activity: during the period of 2017 through 2019, her catalog annually averaged about 256,000 album consumption units, or one-third of 2020’s total. That helps explain the valuation of her catalog when she was shopping the deal, as the assets were at a high-water mark following 2020. And interest remained high, if not as high, in subsequent periods: After the banner year of 2020, Parton’s catalog activity fell to 550,000 album equivalent units in 2021 before rebounding to 610,000 album equivalents in 2022, all figures much higher than pre-pandemic years. Related Will Dolly Parton Earn Her First Billboard 200 No. 1 Album Posthumously? Which brings us to the 2022-2025 period, the years most relevant to a current valuation for Parton’s catalog, as music asset buyers like at least a three-year history of performance when assessing valuations. During that period — which contains the catalog’s best year of the past decade, 2023, when her catalog generated 769,000 album consumption units — her catalog has averaged about 625,000 album equivalent units a year in the U.S., while globally her on-demand stream count averaged 1.16 billion plays. (Overall, since Luminate and its predecessor companies first began tracking sales and other activity in 1991, the Parton catalog has generated 16.5 million album consumption units in the U.S.) How Much Would She See? While Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell told Billboard in August 2020 that her publishing catalog generated $6 million to $8 million a year, based on the above performance of the catalog, Billboard estimates her publishing catalog generated $6.5 million in royalties, nowadays. Separately, Billboard estimates that her master recording catalog generated about $11 million in global revenue annually for the period. In terms of publishing, the revenue from her own recordings averaged almost $5.7 million annually over the past four years, with covers bringing in an additional estimated $800,000 based on information from industry financial sources, adding up to that $6.5 million figure. In terms of her master recordings, sources say Sony Music owns her masters from her RCA period, and also likely from her stint on Columbia Nashville, too, totaling some 23 albums. But in 1995, she issued the first album on her own Blue Eye label — still distributed by Sony — and since then owns most, if not all, of her subsequent studio recordings, or some 17 albums. Consequently, Billboard estimates that about 79% of Parton’s sales and streaming activity comes from masters owned by Sony Music. Applying that percentage against the estimated $11 million in total revenue her masters generate, Sony’s total comes in at $8.6 million, with the titles that Parton owns generating about $2.4 million in revenue. Related Forever No. 1: Dolly Parton, ‘9 to 5’ How much of that would go to Parton? On the recordings side, based on a superstar royalty rate of 33%, she would take home about $2.84 million in net label share from the Sony-owned recordings; of her owned recordings, assuming that she keeps 76% of revenue after production, distribution, marketing and other costs, that would total $1.83 million. The publishing side is more complicated, as might be expected, but given that she owned her own catalog for her entire career, it’s simpler than most: Billboard estimates she has about a 75% share of the 600 or so songs across her 49 albums, which would come out to about $4.25 million from the publishing on her own catalog. When cover songs are factored in — she maintains at least a co-write on more than 3,000 songs, including collaborations and songs written for and/or recorded by others, such as Whitney Houston’s megahit “I Will Always Love You” — that figure rises to an estimated $5 million annually, which, after an estimated 7% administration fee, settles out around $4.67 million. All told, that adds up to $4.6 million in master recording income and $4.67 million from the publishing side for a total average annual take home of $9.27 million. What Could a Buyer Expect to Pay? A superstar multiple of 25 times on $9.27 million in income comes out to almost $232 million, a usually strong indicator of final valuation. However, while Parton has been an iconic superstar, even she likely doesn’t command a 25 times multiple on the passive income — the royalties from her music — from Sony. Related Dolly Parton’s Legacy on the Billboard 200 Chart: 7 Decades of Hit Albums Normally, passive royalties — in which there is no ownership involved — trade on a multiple of 12-16 times, depending on the quality of the song or catalog’s performance. But assuming an iconic superstar rate of 20 times for her $2.84 million in Sony royalties, that would carry a nearly $57 million valuation. And assuming an iconic superstar multiple of 25 times for both her owned master recordings, with take home pay of $1.83 million; and her publishing take home pay of $4.65 million; that would carry valuations of $45.75 million and $116.5 million, respectively. Adding those three valuations together brings us to a total valuation of about $220 million — well in range of the $230 million valuation that industry sources are currently estimating. Sony declined to comment for this story. Parton representatives didn’t respond to a request for comment by press time.

content: Jermaine Dupri has quickly dropped a lawsuit against Sony Music that claimed he was owed $18 million in unpaid royalties tied to albums from Mariah Carey, Usher and others. The legendary hip-hop producer and his So-So Def Recordings sued Sony Music in July, accusing the label of a “systemic pattern” of using “contemptuous accounting practices” to underpay royalties for many years. Related Jermaine Dupri Sues Sony Music for $18M in Unpaid Royalties on Mariah Carey & Usher Albums Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery But less than two months later, attorneys for Dupri moved Friday (Aug. 28) to voluntarily dismiss the case, telling the judge that they had “resolved the matter.” The move did not come with a written explanation, and an attorney for Dupri did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Sony declined to comment. Dupri, who wrote and produced Kris Kross’s 1992 all-timer “Jump,” had a long career as a hit-making producer, helping Carey, Usher, Nelly and others create chart-topping tracks. He also released a pair of studio albums himself, featuring high-profile collab tracks with Jay-Z and Ludacris. The son of former Columbia Records executive Michael Mauldin, Dupri founded So-So Def in 1993 as a joint venture with Columbia and Sony, where he later signed Xscape, Bow Wow, Da Brat and others. That partnership ended in 2002 and, after several more years at Sony imprints, So-So Def hopped from EMI to UMG to several other distributors. In his July lawsuit, Dupri claimed that over a “32-year contractual and business relationship” Sony had repeatedly failed to pay proper royalties to him and his company: “As it turns out, many of SME’s dealings with So-So Def have not been lawful and have harmed So-So Def in its business.” Dupri claimed he was owed more than $2 million for Kris Kross’s first two albums, including their smash, Totally Krossed Out, which featured “Jump.” He also accused Sony of using bookkeeping trickery to maintain unrecouped advances on other music. Friday’s dismissal will end all those accusations without any real litigation. But it came with a catch: Dupri’s lawyers moved to drop the case “without prejudice,” meaning they could theoretically refile it at some point in the future.

content: The second week of the Tupac Shakur murder trial saw an explosive jailhouse recording, prosecutors rest their case and attorneys for Duane “Keffe D” Davis quickly wrap their own brief defense, sending the trial to the jury far sooner than expected. You’re reading Billboard’s weekly Tupac trial recap, a one-sheet breakdown of everything that happened in the epic murder case over the past week. Stay tuned here each Friday for all the testimony and big events you might have missed. Related Tupac Murder Trial Week 1 Recap: An 'Act of Revenge,' Heated Testimony & Police Tapes Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery After a first week filled with fireworks, prosecutors resumed their case on Monday (Aug. 24) with testimony from filmmaker Michael Dorsey, who worked on a BET docuseries in which Davis gave interviews discussing his role in the killing. Jurors watched hours of unedited interview footage, which featured Davis declining to apologize to Tupac’s family. Later in the week, prosecutors called police officers and investigators to the stand, including Robert Ladd, who testified that Davis was a “shot caller” within his Compton gang. Ladd told jurors that Davis’ nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, who allegedly pulled the trigger, could not have opened fire on Tupac without his uncle’s permission: “The younger gang members are supposed to do what they’re told without hesitation.” As prosecutors neared the end of their case, they played a jailhouse recording from 2023 in which Davis uttered a line that the state clearly wanted jurors to remember: “I got blood on my money,” he said in the tape. On Wednesday (Aug. 26), the prosecution rested its case — far sooner than expected for a trial that was anticipated to run for at least four weeks. In total, they had called 24 witnesses and played more than eight hours of recordings, mostly of Davis himself discussing his role in the killing. When the defense kicked off its case on Thursday (Aug. 27), it didn’t last long. They called just three witnesses — all of them former Las Vegas Metropolitan Police officers — in less than two hours, aimed at poking holes and raising reasonable doubt in the mind of jurors. One testified that he saw a light-colored Cadillac arrive leave Suge Knight’s Las Vegas mansion on the night of the crime — seemingly an effort by the defense to suggest that the vehicle used in the crime might have come from Knight’s own entourage. Another faced questions about the quality of the police work on the case, testifying that records had to be locked to avoid interference from “curious” staffers and that some files were later lost. Perhaps more notable was who didn't testify: Davis himself. Defense attorneys rarely put a criminal defendant on the witness stand, since it subjects them to withering cross-examination by prosecutors. And in a case where jurors already heard from him so many times, Davis' attorneys chose not to go against that conventional legal wisdom. With both sides rested, jury instructions were set to be delivered on Friday (Aug. 28) and closing statements are set for the morning on Monday (Aug. 31). After that, the trial — and the fate of the long-unsolved Tupac murder case — will be in the hands of the jurors. The time needed to deliberate in such cases varies widely, from just a few hours to many days, meaning verdict could come as soon as Monday.

content: After more than 30 years of minimal to no use, the city of Portland, Ore., had three ideas for the old building that once housed Washington High School: tear it down, convert it into office buildings space, or — the more out-of-the-box idea — turn it into a music venue. The Washington High building “was a bad investment for anybody, honestly,” says Portland entrepreneur Kevin Cradock, who owns Revolution Hall, Mississippi Studios and Polaris Hall. But local developer and preservationist Art DeMuro had a vision for the long-standing brick building. He envisioned a concert hall within the more than 130,000-square foot facility with additional office spaces in the place of former classrooms. “DeMuro was savvy enough and respected enough and beloved enough that he got the deal done with the city,” backed by real estate developer PacTrust in 2013, Cradock adds. Related Why The Belly Up in San Diego Is a Magnet for Music Royalty — From The Rolling Stones to Snoop Dogg Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery Shortly after securing the high school — which first opened in 1906 and moved to its current location in 1909, then was rebuilt in 1924 following a fire — for an $18 million restoration, DeMuro passed away from cancer. But the project went on, and when it came time to design and build out the concert venue, the development company Venerable Properties reached out to the owners of Portland’s beloved indie venue Mississippi Studios, Cradock and Jim Brunberg, to build what would be called Revolution Hall. “I was having a sandwich next door at this place called Meat Cheese Bread, and Jim just rolled over with our talent buyer at the time and said, ‘Hey, we're gonna go look at this high school. They want to turn it into a music venue,’” says Cradock. “I didn’t even go with them.” Cradock was familiar with the building. Back in his bartending days, he used to break into the high school after work through what he called “the door of debauchery,” and take in the stunning view of the city in the wee hours of the morning. He says that the door was never latched and earlier this year he got the original vestibule he broke in through tattooed on his leg. After the school shut down, Cradock also attended experimental shows called Time-Based Art put on by the Portland Institute of Contemporary Art at the building. At the time, there was no running water, only one usable bathroom on the bottom floor, and the event organizers had to run electricity from a generator. “I think they had permission, but maybe not,” says Brunberg. “It was permission light,” jokes Cradock. “Diet permission.” Revolution Hall in Portland, Ore. Jim Brunberg/Courtesy Revolution Hall By the time DeMuro’s team was ready to renovate Washington High, the whole place needed to be gutted. The restoration project included a historic overlay to preserve the exterior and design elements of the school, but new plumbing and electrical systems were installed, as well as a new roof. Despite the obvious cost and complications of renovating a space that hadn’t seen regular use in over three decades, Cradock and Brunberg, who always have a sawzall or some form of chainsaw in their cars to “tweak” things at one of their venues, were up to the task. Wanting to spend more time at home after years as a touring musician in bands like Box Set (which appeared on the cover of Billboard magazine’s best unsigned bands issue in 1994), Brunberg opened Mississippi Studios in 2003. Originally, the space had been a recording studio, but Brunberg transformed the former church into a 100-cap room that welcomed underplays from Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Brandi Carlile, Regina Spektor, Feist, Rickie Lee Jones and Hot Tuna. A few years later, Brunberg met Cradock at a mutual friend’s party. “I knew who Jim was the whole time, so when he very casually said, ‘The business isn't doing good, I just had these kids and I'm on the road, be my business partner,’ I was like, ‘That sounds like a good idea,’” says Cradock, who had spent years in music-adjacent jobs and in construction. The trust was immediately apparent in their working relationship. “Jim announced to the staff before I even was a legal owner that I was one of the owners, and then he went on the road with [the band] Storm,” says Cradock. Revolution Hall owners Jim Brunberg (left) and Kevin Cradock. Byron Beck/Courtesy Revolution Hall In 2009, Cradock fully jumped in to improve food and beverage options and add structure to the business side of Mississippi Studios. Over the years, Mississippi Studios has been renovated several times and the pair added the Bar Bar restaurant, which claims to have the best burgers in town. “He saved the business because I was a dumbass musician trying to run this little venue,” says Brunberg. “We're like a family. Everybody thinks that Kevin and I are either married or brothers, and that's fine with us.” The jovial duo quickly realized the biggest initial expense in renovating Washington High was soundproofing the auditorium so that the other tenants wouldn’t be disrupted by soundcheck in the middle of the day. And the historic overlay meant even the curved wood auditorium chairs had to keep their original design. Related From ‘Dime-a-Dance' to Hosting U2 & Bob Dylan: How Cain’s Ballroom in Tulsa Has Endured for Over a Century “The old seats were only 16 inches wide, but we did not notice that when we first got the tour of the building,” Brunberg says. Local codes mandate that seats be at least 21 inches wide. On that initial tour, Brunberg laughs that he patted himself on the back for bringing a tape measure to check the length of the seats. “They were 23 inches wide, which is great. But those were the teachers’ seats at the end of the rows.” Alongside local woodworker Matt Lackey, they had to learn to bend plywood and rebuild 500 seats by hand. “We were both spending the night there,” says Brunberg. “I would work on the seats all day and then literally fall asleep on the balcony and Kevin would fall asleep on the floor in the bar because we were trying to just get things open and running a skeleton crew — enlisting our friends and bandmates and family.” They brought in old bowling alley lanes to create two of the four bars throughout the building, which includes the main concert hall and the Assembly Lounge bar on the second floor; a lower-level 200-cap room called the Show Bar; and ground-level cafe Martha’s. Wet Leg at Revolution Hall in Portland, Ore. Jason Quigley/Courtesy Revolution Hall Shortly before the soft and hard openings of Revolution Hall in February and April 2015, respectively, Brunberg and Cradock asked a handful of local musicians to christen the venue by being the first to play music in it. Soul singer and local legend Ural Thomas — a regular at Mississippi Studios — was asked to join. “I wanted [Rev Hall] to have his blessing,” says Brunberg, who had the pleasure of attending the then-75-year-old's local jam sessions. “He said, ‘I want to sing my mom’s favorite song.’ He teared up and sang “Danny Boy.’” Revolution Hall opened its doors to the public with two nights of Neko Case in April 2015 and has since welcomed Indigo Girls, Cat Power, Kim Gordon, Kathleen Hanna, Kurt Vile, Robert Glasper, Tegan and Sara, Lindsey Buckingham, Nick Cave, Buddy Guy, Pennywise, Laufey, Jack White, Sleater-Kinney, Wet Leg, Jeff Tweedy and Mavis Staples. The talent buying team (Trevor Solomon, Lori Hughes Killen and Theo Craig) at the promotion and booking arm of Mississippi Studios, True West, “are great people and the shows they’ve gotten for the venue have been really innovative and outside the box sometimes,” says Brunberg. “But also they can do the mainstream.” The True West team not only books talent for Mississippi Studios and Revolution Hall, but also Show Bar and Polaris Hall, which is a former progressive women’s hall-turned-290-capacity music venue. In addition, earlier this year, Rev Hall’s rooftop bar was completed and can host the occasional small show. From April to October, the renovated Roof Deck (the same space Cradock had tattooed) is open to the public and “one of Portland’s most popular tourist attractions,” says Cradock. The Roof Deck is the 10th bar they’ve built across their three locations and they consider it an economic imperative to have as many concession spaces as possible, especially ones open to the public on non-show nights. “Ticket sales won’t ever pay all the bills. You need a robust concession program. You need private events,” says Cradock. “But the reason that we are there is not because of the margaritas. It’s because of the music.”

content: Spotify has promoted Joe Hadley to vp of global music content and partnerships, where he will now run both the music editorial and partnerships teams. Along with the move, J.J. Italiano will also become head of editorial, which encompasses global music curation, North American editorial and the company’s overall editorial strategy. "Editorial is a key part of bringing an essential human touch to Spotify," Charlie Hellman, senior vp and global head of music at Spotify, said in a statement. "The team’s judgment and taste is what fans and artists rely on. Joe’s capable leadership will keep artist advocacy at the center of our work and bring even more impact to the programming we do." Related Spotify to Label AI Artists on the Platform With New 'AI Persona' Badge Dale Morris, Nashville Manager Who Guided Careers of Alabama & Kenny Chesney, Dies at 89 HYBE Pledges Over $300k for Colombia Earthquake Recovery Within the last 12 months, Spotify has seen major changes within its leadership structure. Last September, the company’s founder, Daniel Ek, announced that he was transitioning from his role as CEO to executive chairman. Gustav Söderström and Alex Norström, who had been co-presidents, stepped in as co-CEOs of the company. Both Söderström and Norström report to Ek. Additionally, global head of editorial Sulinna Ong left to take a role on U2's management team. On Aug. 11, Spotify announced the company’s plans to label AI artists on the platform with an "AI Persona" badge. Artists who are tagged with the label will be excluded from personalized recommendations on the streaming service. In April, Spotify held its Investors Day presentation, where the company announced a licensing deal with Universal Music Group for AI remixes on the streaming platform. (On Aug. 4, Merlin also signed a licensing agreement for the same tool.) Their Investors Day conference also saw the announcement of Spotify Reserved, a service in partnership with Live Nation that allows fans a chance to purchase tickets to see their favorite artists perform.

content: The iconic Reason Rack has been a core component of the Reason DAW since its launch in 2000. But in 2019, it was made available as a standalone plugin for the first time, offering producers the chance to harness its power within DAWs outside of Reason. Reason Rack is highly acclaimed, and allows producers to stack virtual instruments on top of one another with total control over the routing between them. Now, Reason Studios has unveiled a new free version, offering 15 Reason instruments, effects and creative utilities for no cost at all. This isn’t a trial, and has no expiration or watermark, Reason confirms. READ MORE: Polyend has unveiled a new MIDI controller – and it looks an awful lot like a QWERTY keyboard Reason Free – what’s actually included? Credit: Reason Studios The 15 included Devices consist of four virtual instruments, five effects, and six creative utilities. The flagship virtual instrument available within Reason Free is Europa, a powerful wavetable synthesizer geared towards “modern sound design”, with three spectral engineers, advanced waveform shaping, modulation and effects, and a bank of over 600 presets for instant inspiration. The full list of included Devices is below: Instruments Europa – Powerful wavetable synthesizer for modern sound design Kong – Versatile drum machine for beats, samples and percussion ID8 – All-in-one collection of essential songwriting instruments Monotone – Monophonic synthesizer for deep basses and expressive lead Effects Scream 4 – Creative distortion and saturation The Echo – Flexible stereo delay with modulation and filtering Audiomatic – One-knob effect for vintage and lo-fi character RV7000 MkII – Professional reverb for realistic and creative spaces MClass Maximizer – Mastering limiter for louder, cleaner mixes Creative utilities Scales & Chords – Creates melodies and chords that stay in key Combinator – Combines instruments and effects into custom devices Pulsar – Dual modulation device for adding movement to any Rack parameter Spider Audio Merger & Splitter – Splits and combines audio signals Spider CV Merger & Splitter – Routes and combines modulation signals MIDI Out Device – Controls external plugins and hardware How is Reason Free different from the full Reason Rack? Where Reason Free offers 15 instruments, effects and utilities, the full Reason Rack – included in a Reason+ subscription – offers more than 90, as well as weekly Sound Packs, plus access to the full Reason DAW. Also included in Reason+ is access to the LANDR ecosystem, with unlimited music distribution and tools for creativity, mixing and mastering. Additionally, Reason users can expand their setup with individual Rack Extensions and Refills, or by buying a perpetual Reason licence. What is Reason Studios saying about Reason Free? Credit: Reason Studios “Reason has always been about musical exploration – when you connect two Devices, turn the knobs, and discover a great sound you weren’t looking for,” says Mattias Häggström Gerdt, Product Manager at Reason Studios. “With Reason Free, we’re giving everyone a piece of that experience. The included Devices are fantastic in their own right, but the Rack also gives you the freedom to go deeper, experiment and build something entirely your own.” Pricing & availability As the name might suggest, Reason Free is totally free, and is available now as a VST3, AU and AAX plugin for compatible DAWS. “It is free forever, with no trial period, expiration date or watermark,” Reason Studios says. Additionally, Reason Free can run as a DAW of its own, offering producers up to 16 tracks. Learn more at Reason Studios. content: A US judge has allowed UMG and Sony to pursue Suno over alleged YouTube ‘stream ripping’ to train its AI models. Here's what artists need to know. A US judge has allowed Universal Music Group and Sony Music to add a new claim against AI music company Suno, alleging it bypassed YouTube's technology to download copyrighted recordings for AI training. Here's what the case could mean for musicians, producers and the future of AI-generated music. The legal battle between the music industry and AI music generators has taken another significant turn. A US federal judge has given Universal Music Group (UMG) and Sony Music Entertainment permission to pursue a claim accusing Suno of using so-called “stream ripping” to obtain copyrighted recordings from YouTube and use them to train its AI music models. The decision doesn't mean Suno has been found guilty of piracy. Instead, Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV has ruled that the labels have presented a plausible enough case for the claim to move forward while the court examines the evidence. For musicians and producers, however, the development is significant. The case highlights one of the biggest questions surrounding generative AI in music: where does the training data come from, and should artists be paid or asked for permission when their recordings are used? What is ‘stream ripping’? The term might sound technical, but the basic idea is fairly straightforward. The labels allege that Suno obtained music from YouTube by using software designed to download audio from online videos. Their amended complaint names open-source tools including YT-DL and YT-DLP, alleging that Suno used them to bypass YouTube's technical protections and extract copyrighted recordings. At the centre of the new claim is YouTube's “rolling cipher”, a technical measure that the labels say is designed to prevent unauthorised access to underlying media files. The labels argue that bypassing this technology amounts to circumvention under Section 1201(a)(1) of the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA). Suno has previously disputed the legal basis of this argument, including questioning whether the technology in question actually controls access to the copyrighted works in the way required by the DMCA. Judge Saylor said determining exactly how the technology and downloading tools work will require more evidence. For now, though, he found that the labels' allegations were sufficient to proceed. This is separate from the bigger copyright question It's worth making a distinction here. UMG and Sony are already suing Suno over the alleged use of copyrighted sound recordings to train its AI system. The stream-ripping claim is an additional legal argument focused specifically on how the recordings were allegedly obtained. The court has not yet decided whether Suno's use of copyrighted recordings to train its AI model constitutes fair use. That question remains one of the central issues in the case, with fact discovery scheduled to close on September 30, 2026, according to the latest reporting. The parties are then expected to seek summary judgment on the wider question of whether training an AI model on copyrighted recordings without a licence can qualify as fair use. In other words, there's still a lot to be decided. Why this matters to independent artists For independent musicians, this isn't simply another major-label legal dispute. The argument over AI training affects anyone whose music is publicly available online. Independent artists often upload their music to YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud and other platforms specifically because they want people to hear it. But being publicly available doesn't necessarily mean an artist has agreed for their recordings to be downloaded, copied and incorporated into an AI training dataset. That's one of the biggest tensions in the current AI debate. Listening to a song and using a song to build a commercial AI model are two very different things. The music industry is increasingly asking where that line should be drawn. Independent artists are already taking Suno to court The major labels aren't the only rights holders pursuing Suno. Country artist Tony Justice, alongside his label and publishing company, has brought a proposed class action against Suno representing independent artists, songwriters and producers. In August, Judge Saylor refused to dismiss most of that case, allowing claims involving alleged AI output infringement and the alleged circumvention of YouTube's technology to proceed. The case is particularly relevant to independent musicians because the plaintiffs argue that creators outside the major-label system also need meaningful protection as AI companies build increasingly powerful music-generation tools. That could make the coming months particularly important for independent artists. The music industry is moving towards licensing Interestingly, while Suno continues to face litigation, the company is also beginning to move towards licensed music. In August, Suno announced a deal with BMG covering recorded music and publishing repertoire, with the agreement described as opt-in for artists and songwriters and intended to settle Suno's previous use of BMG's catalogue. Suno has also said that it plans to introduce a new generation of models “developed in partnership with the music industry”, while retiring its previous models. That shift could prove important. Rather than the industry having to decide whether AI music should exist at all, the bigger question may increasingly become what a fair AI music ecosystem looks like. That could include licensing agreements, artist opt-in systems, compensation models and clearer rules around training data. AI isn't going away, but the rules are changing The Suno case comes at a time when governments, streaming services, record companies and artists are all trying to establish where AI fits into the music industry. Recent developments have included streaming platforms introducing greater transparency around AI-generated music, while Australia's ARIA Charts has moved to exclude fully AI-generated recordings from chart eligibility. Meanwhile, a German court recently ruled that Suno infringed copyright by processing songs without the necessary rights in a case brought by German collecting society GEMA. Suno has said it is considering its options, including an appeal. The direction of travel is becoming increasingly clear: AI companies are going to face more questions about where their training material comes from. What should artists be doing? For independent artists, there's no need to panic or stop using AI tools altogether. Instead, be more careful about understanding the tools you're using. Before incorporating AI-generated material into a commercial release, check the platform's terms around ownership, commercial use, training data and licensing. Keep track of how your music is created, particularly if you're using AI alongside your own recordings or production. It's also worth keeping your original project files, stems and recordings. As AI identification and rights-management systems become more sophisticated, having a clear record of your creative process could become increasingly useful. And, as always, make sure your music is properly registered and distributed with accurate metadata. The bigger picture for musicians Perhaps the most important takeaway from the Suno case is that the AI music debate is moving beyond “Can AI make music?” It clearly can. The harder questions are now about ownership, consent, compensation and transparency. If an AI company can legally license music from artists and rights holders to train its models, there is a potential path towards an ecosystem where technology and human creativity can coexist. But if copyrighted music can simply be scraped from the internet and used without permission, independent artists could find themselves competing with systems trained on the very music they spent years creating. That's why this case matters even if you've never used Suno. The decisions being made now could influence how music is created, distributed and monetised for years to come. For independent artists, the best response is to stay informed, understand where AI fits into your own workflow and keep building your catalogue and audience. content: Released a new song and the streams aren't coming in? Don't panic. Here's how independent artists can turn a disappointing release into useful momentum for the next one. Releasing new music is exciting, but it can also be a little brutal. You spend weeks or months writing, recording, mixing and preparing a track, only to see surprisingly few streams once it finally goes live. Before you decide the song has failed, take a breath. Low streams don't necessarily mean you've made a bad song. For independent artists, getting music heard is often a gradual process, and one release rarely tells the full story. Give your release time It's easy to obsess over the numbers during the first few days, but don't treat release day as a final verdict. Unless you already have a large audience waiting for your music, it can take time for a track to reach new listeners. Instead of asking why your song hasn't gone viral, think about whether you've given people enough opportunities to discover it. One Instagram post announcing your release probably isn't enough. Keep the song active across your social channels and look for different ways to introduce it. Share the story behind the track, post a performance, show how you produced a particular section or highlight a lyric you love. You don't need to repeat the same promotional message over and over; find different stories within the same release. Look beyond the stream count Streams are an obvious metric, but they're not the only indication that your music is connecting with people. Look at saves, follows, playlist additions, comments and repeat listeners. A smaller number of genuinely engaged listeners can be far more valuable than thousands of passive plays. Your analytics can also help you understand where people are discovering your music. If listeners are coming from your artist profile, playlists, social media or algorithmic recommendations, each tells you something different about your audience and promotional strategy. Use that information rather than simply refreshing your stream count. Don't forget about the song itself Sometimes your promotion needs improving. Sometimes the song simply hasn't found the right audience yet. Think about who your track is actually for. Are you putting it in front of people who already listen to your genre? Are you working with other artists or creators who have a similar audience? Are you submitting to relevant playlists rather than simply chasing the biggest numbers? The goal isn't to get your song in front of everyone. It's to get it in front of the right listeners. And don't be tempted by services promising thousands of guaranteed streams. Artificial streams don't create fans and can put your release at risk with streaming platforms. Building an audience might take longer, but genuine listeners are what you actually want. Keep the song alive Your release doesn't have to disappear after the first week. If you still believe in the track, keep finding new ways to present it. Perform it live, create an acoustic version, share a behind-the-scenes clip or revisit it when you have a new idea for content. A song can find its audience weeks or even months after release. Music doesn't suddenly become irrelevant because it didn't perform immediately. For independent artists, this is particularly important. Without a major label campaign constantly pushing your music, you have to give your strongest songs room to breathe. Use the experience to improve your next release Every release is an experiment. Maybe your best-performing content was a simple studio clip rather than an expensive music video. Perhaps listeners responded strongly to one particular part of the song. You might discover that one platform consistently sends more engaged listeners than another. Take note. Your next release can benefit from everything you've learned from the previous one. This is also where having a reliable distribution strategy matters. Making sure your music is correctly delivered across the major streaming and social platforms gives potential listeners more opportunities to discover you. RouteNote helps independent artists and labels distribute their music while retaining control over their releases. One quiet release doesn't define your career It's easy to attach your emotions to a number. But a song getting 200 streams instead of 2,000 doesn't mean you've failed. Building a music career is usually about consistency, experimentation and gradually finding your audience. Some releases will perform better than others. Some songs will surprise you. content: SoundCloud has spent years being the place where you stumble across your next favourite artist. Now, it wants to be the place where you actually buy their music, too. The company is currently testing a new feature that lets artists sell and deliver music directly from their SoundCloud profiles, meaning fans can discover a track, decide they want to own it and buy the download without being sent off to another platform. Artists can set their own prices and offer music in formats including MP3 and WAV. More importantly, SoundCloud takes no commission from those sales. Once standard fees and taxes are deducted, artists keep 100% of the revenue. READ MORE: How to get playlisted on streaming services: 7 playlist pitching tips It’s a notable addition to a platform that has traditionally been much better at getting music heard than getting it sold. A stream might introduce an artist to a new fan, but a direct purchase puts actual money into the artist’s pocket. SoundCloud says there’s already a sizeable appetite for that. Around 250,000 artists currently direct fans to external platforms to buy their music, with 2.4 million tracks linked to purchase pages. The company says more than 500,000 SoundCloud users are sent to those external sites every year, while 28% of surveyed artists either already sell downloadable music or want to start. The feature will initially be tested with 200 US-based Artist Pro creators. Feedback from the beta will help shape the service before it rolls out to all eligible creators later this autumn. Participating artists will be able to monitor their sales through Artist Studio and the Fan Support Dashboard. Direct sales will also add to SoundCloud’s existing artist monetisation tools, including Fan-Powered Royalties, Fan Support, on-demand vinyl and ticketing. “Artists should be able to build their audience in one place, on one platform,” says SoundCloud CEO Eliah Seton. “SoundCloud has always been where artists find their first fans and build real communities. We’re continuing to bring more of what they need to grow their careers into that same experience, while letting fans directly support the music they love.” SoundCloud’s move follows the lead of Bandcamp, which has long championed direct-to-fan music sales and launched its Bandcamp Fridays initiative in 2020. content: Criminal charges have been dismissed against the man accused of stalking Sabrina Carpenter after a judge ruled him mentally incompetent. According to the Los Angeles City Attorney's Office, a judge overruled prosecutors’ objections on Tuesday (Aug. 25) and held that 31-year-old William Applegate is too mentally unwell to stand trial. Applegate is still subject to a restraining order that requires him to stay away from Carpenter for five years. The pop star alleged in a May legal petition that Applegate, “a complete stranger,” had surveilled her L.A. home for a month before attempting to break in. The singer said Applegate falsely claimed to know her personally, “indicative of a dangerous, delusional and irrational fixation on me.” “The totality of Applegate’s conduct has caused me significant and ongoing fear for my personal safety and the safety of all individuals residing in my home,” wrote Carpenter in a court declaration. “Applegate has repeatedly and willfully violated the sanctity and security of my private residence. His act of physically attempting to open and enter my front door, without invitation, consent or any lawful basis is among the most disturbing violations of personal safety and privacy I have ever experienced.” Applegate opposed Carpenter’s requested restraining order, insisting that he and Carpenter are part of the same “classified military-government program.” In June, a judge in downtown L.A. ordered Applegate to stay at least 100 yards away from the singer’s home, car and workplaces until 2031. The following day, Applegate was criminally charged with eight misdemeanor counts including stalking, disorderly conduct, battery and trespassing. But after a psychiatric evaluation, a different judge in Hollywood threw out those criminal charges due to mental incompetency on Tuesday. Applegate’s attorneys and reps for Carpenter did not immediately return requests for comment on the matter on Thursday (Aug. 27). While stalking has long been a disturbing consequence of fame, the problem has worsened in recent years due to social media; fans now interact more directly with their favorite artists, which can lead to unhealthy obsession for those with mental illness. The internet has also made it easier for stalkers to locate their targets. This has increasingly led artists like Carpenter to seek legal intervention. Multiple individuals have been criminally charged over the last decade with stalking Taylor Swift, who also got a restraining order against another stalker last year. This past April, a woman named Michelle Dick was charged with physically attacking Fleetwood Mac frontman Lindsey Buckingham after years of threats. Like Applegate, Dick has since been ruled mentally incompetent to stand trial.

content: In 2026, labels have access to more data than ever. From streaming trends and playlist activity to territory growth, UGC performance, royalties, and more, that level of information can become overwhelming to the untrained eye. Especially when you're managing multiple artists and releases at a time, you need to know which numbers are actually worth paying attention to. Some metrics show momentum. Some show when attention is starting to shift elsewhere. Others point to new emerging markets, backend issues, or an opportunity for growth that needs attention before the moment passes. The best labels in the game understand not only what to look at, but what that information is telling them and how to use it to make better decisions across their roster. In this post, we’re breaking down 7 metrics every label owner should check weekly, where to find them, and how to use them to keep everyone moving in the right direction… Key Takeaways Weekly change matters more than the biggest number. A smaller track accelerating quickly may deserve more attention than a larger release that is holding steady or declining. Never evaluate a spike by itself. Compare streams with playlist activity, territory growth, UGC, saves, audience behavior, and platform performance to understand what is actually driving momentum. Look for signals that repeat across platforms. When the same city, audience, song section, or behavior appears across streaming, social, video, merch, or ticketing data, you have stronger evidence of a real opportunity. Turn every meaningful metric into a next action. Growth in a territory might justify localized promotion, while strong YouTube activity, playlist traction, or UGC may call for completely different support. Operational data deserves the same attention as marketing data. Reviewing splits, payees, recoupments, royalties, and payouts every week can prevent small backend issues from becoming larger artist relationship problems. What Your Weekly Label Data Is Really Telling You Weekly Stream Movement Streams are usually the first place labels look, but the real value isn’t only in the total number. What you really want to pay attention to every week is how your active releases, artists, and catalog are moving overall. Is an active release gaining week over week? Did one artist’s catalog spike suddenly? Did the whole release drop after promo ended? Are streams shifting between partners, playlists, or territories? This gives you the weekly pulse of your label before you zoom in on individual tracks. For example, one release with 75,000 streams this week may look like the obvious priority at first glance… But if it had 150,000 streams last week, you need to figure out what changed before you put more energy behind it. Did it lose a playlist placement? Did release-week promo end? Did paid spend stop? Did one territory drop off? If the stream drop came from one playlist, you may need to shift focus toward content, user playlists, or another round of pitching. If the drop happened across every platform and territory, the release may need a completely new creative angle before more budget makes sense. On the other hand, a song that jumped from 4,000 streams to 12,000 streams in a week may be showing early traction. That’s when you dig into where the growth came from. For example, if most of the increase came from Mexico City, you can test localized ads, pitch regional playlists, or have the artist post content that speaks directly to that audience. If the growth came from YouTube, check if fans are using the song in videos or if a creator posted something that drove people back to the track. If you’re a Symphonic client, you can check this in your SymphonicMS account under Analytics, then Streams. From there, you can view daily stream data across your catalog and break it down by partner, artist, track, release, playlist, and territory. The whole point of checking this metric is to spot the biggest shifts across the label first, then decide where you need to look closer. Top Tracks by Growth After you check overall stream movement, look at which individual tracks increased the most from the previous week. Not just the tracks with the highest total streams, but the ones that saw the biggest jump compared to where they were before. This can help you catch momentum early, especially across a larger roster. A smaller track going from 1,000 to 5,000 streams in a week may need more attention than a bigger track holding steady at 80,000. When you see that kind of jump, look into where it came from. If it came from a playlist, check how long the placement has been active and if the track is still growing outside of that playlist. If it came from one city or country, consider localized content, ads, or pitching. If it came from YouTube, TikTok, or UGC, find the post, creator, or usage pattern that started the increase and build around it. You can find this in the same place as your weekly stream movement in SymphonicMS under Analytics > Streams. From there, review track-level performance and use the partner, territory, playlist, artist, and release filters to understand where the growth is coming from. Playlist Activity Playlist activity is one of the easiest metrics to misread. A playlist add can give a song a real boost, but it can also make a release look bigger than it actually is if most of the streams are coming from one place. Instead of only looking at the stream spike, look at what happened around it: Did the song keep growing after the playlist add? Did listeners save it or add it to their own playlists? Did the placement lead to more streams across the artist’s catalog? Did the track start moving in new territories? Did the lift continue after the playlist placement ended? In the same place you checked stream movement and track growth in SymphonicMS, you can also see playlist details like track position, playlist streams, and how the placement is changing over time. So if a playlist is driving streams for a few days and everything drops right back down after, that placement may have helped with exposure, but just not deeper fan movement… That’s not necessarily a “bad” thing. It just means the track might need stronger artist-led content, a better follow-up post, another pitching angle, or more support around the part of the song people are reacting to. If the playlist activity leads to saves, followers, user playlist adds, catalog listening, or growth on other platforms, that’s a stronger sign the placement is actually helping the song reach people who will stick around. —— Want to learn more? When this happens, look closer. This could be a sign that a new audience is forming naturally in that market, and a little extra support there could make all the difference. Genres like Latin, Afrobeats, Caribbean, dancehall, electronic, hip-hop, metal, and other communities don’t move the same way in every market. A track may hit first in the artist’s home country, but it can also start growing somewhere completely different because of a playlist, creator trend, local scene, DJ support, diaspora audience, or fan community that picks it up early. When you’re in your SymphonicMS account, take a moment to check the territory breakdowns. Next, compare what you’re seeing there with Spotify for Artists, YouTube Studio, TikTok for Artists, Meta, Bandsintown, Shopify, or even your ticketing data. If the same cities keep showing up across streams, social engagement, video views, merch orders, and show interest, that market deserves a closer look. From there, now you have a real market to build around. Test a small ad budget, pitch regional playlists, reach out to local creators, or shape content around the audience that’s already responding. Want to learn more about building from international traction? Check out How To Monetize Your Music in New Global Markets as an Independent Artist to learn how to turn this early traction into real growth. Partner and Platform Performance When you’re managing multiple releases, artists, and campaigns at once, you can’t go full throttle on every platform for every song. A track may be doing most of its streaming on Spotify, but getting stronger engagement on YouTube. Another may be steady overall, but quietly overperforming on Apple Music, Audiomack, Beatport, Pandora, or another platform that better matches the genre. Checking partner performance helps you see where the release is getting the clearest response; then you can shape the next moves around that. In SymphonicMS, look at your partner breakdowns alongside your track, playlist, and territory data. Look for: Which platform is driving the most activity Which DSP is growing faster than the others Which genre-specific platforms are showing early movement Which platforms are performing better in certain territories Which platform response lines up with the support you’re already giving the release From there, the next move should be a lot clearer. A song gaining on YouTube may need more video support. A track picking up on Beatport may need DJ-focused promo. A release overperforming on one DSP in a specific territory may need more local pitching instead of another broad campaign. Let the data guide you. Social and UGC Activity Social and UGC activity shows how people are using the music, not just listening to it. That could mean a Reel with the hook, a fan edit on YouTube, a TikTok using the beat drop, or an older track getting picked up because one lyric fits a moment. Pay attention to what repeats. If multiple creators keep using the same lyric, intro, beat drop, or emotional part of the song, that gives you something to build around. Don’t force the campaign around the chorus if people are naturally reacting to the first 10 seconds. Also look at who is responding. Age, gender, location, and audience behavior across socials and DSPs can help you understand who the campaign is actually reaching and how to target the next move. A track may be getting strong UGC from younger listeners on TikTok, but stronger streaming activity from 25-34 year-olds on Spotify or YouTube. That can shape your ad targeting, content style, playlist strategy, and which markets you prioritize next. You can also check YouTube UGC and Meta Analytics in your SymphonicMS account to see how your catalog is being used across user-generated content. From there, compare it with TikTok for Artists, YouTube Studio, Instagram Insights, Spotify for Artists, or Shazam. Look at available audience data too, like age ranges, top cities, saves, profile visits, watch behavior, and repeat engagement. If UGC is growing but the streams are flat, the content may not be pushing people to the song yet. If UGC, streams, saves, Shazams, profile visits, and audience trends are all moving together, that’s a stronger sign the content is helping people find the music and take another step with it. Royalty, Split, and Payout Health This is the less glamorous side of running a label, but it’s one of the most important metrics to check every week. Strong streaming numbers don’t mean much if splits are wrong, payees are missing information, recoupments aren’t updated, or royalty details haven’t been reviewed. In SymphonicMS, check your Royalty Summary, SplitShare, and payout details to make sure everything is tracking correctly. Look for anything that could slow down or complicate payments. Things like: Missing payee information Incorrect splits Recoupments that need review Unusual adjustments Releases that aren’t earning the way you expected This is also where you can compare activity to revenue. A track may have fewer streams but stronger earnings because of where those streams came from. Another release may be getting a lot of activity but not generating the kind of revenue you expected, which means it’s worth looking closer at partner, territory, or rights details. For labels, especially, this is also about trust. Artists and collaborators want to know they’re being paid correctly and on time. Checking this weekly helps you catch small issues before they turn into bigger conversations later. Some Final Thoughts… Checking your metrics weekly doesn’t mean obsessing over every small change. It means staying close enough to your catalog to understand what needs your attention before the moment passes. When you know what’s moving, where it’s moving, and what might be causing it, you can make better calls across your roster. You know when to keep pushing a release, when to adjust the strategy, when to support a new market, when to clean up a payout issue, and when to let the data lead you somewhere different altogether. Great label management comes down to paying attention and staying informed about the industry. The numbers won’t make the decisions for you, but they can absolutely show you where to look next. Good luck! Frequently Asked Questions Which music metrics should an independent label check every week? Independent labels should monitor weekly stream movement, top tracks by growth, playlist activity, territory growth, partner and platform performance, social and UGC activity, and royalty, split, and payout health. The most useful insights come from comparing these metrics together rather than judging any one number on its own. How can a label tell whether a streaming spike is real momentum? A streaming spike is more meaningful when other signals rise with it. Look for increases in saves, user playlist adds, UGC, catalog streams, followers, Shazams, or activity in new territories. If streams jump because of one playlist and fall immediately when the placement ends, that may be temporary exposure rather than lasting audience growth. How should labels decide which tracks deserve more marketing support? Look at the rate of growth, not just total streams. A track climbing from 1,000 to 5,000 weekly streams may represent a stronger emerging opportunity than a larger track holding steady at 80,000. Then identify what caused the increase, such as a playlist, territory, creator, platform, or piece of content, before deciding where to put more budget or promotion. When should a label invest more heavily in a new territory? A single week of stronger streams is worth investigating, but repeated signals make the opportunity much stronger. If the same city or country keeps appearing across streaming growth, social engagement, video views, Shazams, merch sales, ticketing interest, or fan activity, it may be time to test localized ads, regional playlist pitching, creator outreach, or market-specific content. What should a label do when UGC is growing, but streams are not? First, identify what people are actually reacting to, such as a lyric, beat drop, intro, or creator trend. Then look at whether the content gives viewers a clear path back to the song or artist. Growing UGC with flat streams can mean the content is resonating socially without yet converting into deeper listening behavior. How often should an independent label review royalties and payout information? A weekly operational check can help catch missing payee information, incorrect splits, outdated recoupments, unusual adjustments, or unexpected revenue patterns before they become bigger issues. Labels should also compare revenue with streaming activity because the releases generating the most streams are not always the ones generating the strongest earnings. How long should a label wait before changing strategy based on weekly data? Not every week-over-week movement calls for an immediate strategy change. First determine whether the shift is isolated or showing up across multiple signals. A sudden playlist loss may explain a short-term decline, while several weeks of falling streams, weaker engagement, and declining platform activity may point to a broader slowdown that deserves a new approach. The software synthesiser experts focused on weight, impact, and motion with this new design. A press release from the team ahead of the Pure SUB release reads: “In modern electronic music, from dubstep and drum & bass to the wider world of club and bass-driven production, low-end has become the defining voice. READ MORE: Dreamtonics’ Instrument X can create a digital orchestra that sounds like real musicians “Over the past decade, bass has moved from the foundation under the track toward the front of it. It’s not unusual now for a producer to spend hours on a single sub - sculpting harmonics, distortion and movement until the bass is the hook, the signature, the drop. “With the rise of sound design as a craft, a sound once felt and forgotten is now designed with the care once reserved for the lead. Pure SUB is a synthesiser built for that one job.” Included in Pure SUB is a three-way split between sub, harmonics, and texture which can “morph timbre through a dual-mode engine built for everything from clean 808s to wide Reese, then blend in noise and texture so the bass cuts through on any system”. The new kit will also reshape harmonics through more than 40 filter modes. Arturia adds that this will “drive the timbre with the Sub Processor - a bass-focused chain of expert-built modes that distort, texturise and transform in a few moves”. New motion tools are also featured as part of the Pure SUB kit which offers three envelopes, six customisable modulators and full keyboard expressivity. This includes MPE, layer samples and noise, animation for any parameter, and modulation even to the modulators themselves. Pure SUB will also have new tools for distorting in the FX rack, a preset randomiser to offer up new ideas with its “instant new sound” option, and a resampling tool that can give every note or bounce a “slightly different” sound. These changeable keys are also backlit. The company also says it's looking into making the firmware behind Keys open source. “Alternative layouts, different control modes, custom MIDI tools, sequencers, and other ideas can all be explored through software,” it says. It can also be used as a standalone controller. “Nine rotary controls can be freely assigned to MIDI CCs for controlling software or hardware, or mapped to everyday computer functions like volume, scrolling, and brightness. A built-in display gives you feedback as you make adjustments,” the brand continues. Polyend says Keys is still in its prototype phase, so “functionality, colour, or hardware could change”.
