content: Luminate is introducing a new framework designed to identify and measure AI-generated music, with ‘AI Generated’ labels coming to its CONNECT platform later this year. For independent artists, labels and distributors, the move could signal a new era of transparency around how AI is used in music. AI-generated music is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Streaming platforms are receiving enormous volumes of AI-created tracks, while artists, labels and rights holders are trying to understand how this rapidly expanding catalogue is affecting discovery, royalties, charts and the wider music ecosystem. Now, one of the music industry's most important data companies is taking a major step towards making that activity easier to track. Luminate has launched a new framework for identifying and measuring AI-generated music, with its CONNECT platform now capable of flagging AI-generated songs and artists worldwide. The new labels are expected to become visible to CONNECT customers and partners later in 2026. For independent musicians and labels, this is another important development in an industry where transparency around AI is quickly becoming part of the normal release process. What is Luminate's new AI music framework? Luminate is best known for its music consumption data, with its information helping power Billboard's charts and providing industry professionals with insight into streaming, sales and audience behaviour. Its CONNECT platform brings together data on artists, songs and releases, allowing music companies to analyse performance, consumption and market trends. The new AI framework adds another layer to that system. Luminate says CONNECT can now identify AI-generated songs and artists, with the company having already identified thousands of AI-generated items in its database. The classifications aren't visible to users yet, but Luminate says the labels will roll out to customers and partners later this year. Songs and recordings identified as fully AI-created will receive an “AI Generated” label. There will also be separate classifications for artists. An “AI” label will indicate an artist confirmed to be fully AI-generated, while “Human” will only be applied to artists individually confirmed by Luminate's screening process. Importantly, Luminate says that a lack of an AI or Human label doesn't necessarily mean something has been confirmed as human-made. The company hasn't yet processed its entire database through the identification system. How will Luminate identify AI-generated music? Rather than relying on one detection method, Luminate is building its framework around three different sources of information. The first is Luminate's own identification technology. Its data science team analyses artists and songs in CONNECT, looking at streaming data and metadata before using audio identification technology to help confirm potential AI-generated material. The second element is data supplied by streaming platforms. As DSPs develop their own systems for identifying AI-generated music, Luminate says it will be able to incorporate that information through its existing partnerships. The third is attribution information from AI music companies themselves. Luminate says it is in discussions with AI music companies about receiving information directly from the source, potentially allowing AI-generated content to be identified before it reaches a streaming service. That combination could eventually give the industry a much clearer picture of how AI-generated music moves from creation to distribution to consumption. Why does this matter now? The timing is significant. AI-generated music has grown at a remarkable pace, creating a challenge for platforms and rights holders trying to distinguish between human-made, AI-assisted and fully AI-generated music. Luminate CEO Rob Jonas said the growth of AI music has moved faster than the industry's ability to consistently identify and measure it, arguing that greater visibility is needed to understand trends, assess fraud risks and make informed decisions. The scale of the issue has become increasingly obvious. In July, Deezer said it was receiving close to 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks per day in June, accounting for more than half of new tracks delivered to the service on peak days. That's a huge amount of music entering the ecosystem. And while AI music itself isn't necessarily a problem, the sheer volume creates questions about discovery, streaming manipulation and how royalties are distributed. For independent artists, that's where the issue becomes particularly relevant. AI music isn't automatically the problem It's important to separate AI-assisted music creation from music that is generated almost entirely by AI. Many human artists already use AI tools in some part of their creative process. They might use AI for brainstorming, sound design, mastering, editing, production assistance or other elements of their workflow. That doesn't necessarily mean the finished recording is an entirely AI-generated work. Luminate's current framework is specifically focused on identifying recordings that are fully AI-created, while its artist classifications are intended to identify artists that are fully AI-generated. That's an important distinction for musicians. The conversation around AI is moving beyond the simple question of whether an artist has used AI at all. Increasingly, the industry will need to understand how AI was used, how much of a recording was generated by it and where human creativity remains central. That could become increasingly important for artists as platforms develop their own AI policies. Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms are also moving towards AI labels Luminate's announcement is part of a much wider industry trend. Streaming platforms have started developing their own approaches to AI transparency, with Deezer already identifying and tagging AI-generated music. Apple Music announced in August that it will label songs that are materially generated using AI, while Spotify has announced an “AI Persona” badge for artist profiles built around AI-generated identities. Spotify also says music from those AI Personas will be kept out of editorial and algorithmic recommendations by default. That means AI disclosure is increasingly moving from being something discussed by industry organisations into something listeners may actually see. For artists, that's worth paying attention to. The metadata attached to your music is becoming more important, and transparency around how a track was created could increasingly influence how it is treated by platforms and industry databases. Could AI labels affect the charts? This is where Luminate's announcement becomes particularly interesting. Luminate provides the data behind Billboard's charts, meaning the company's ability to identify AI-generated music could eventually have implications for how AI tracks are measured within the wider music industry. However, Luminate has not said that its AI labels automatically determine chart eligibility. That's an important distinction. Billboard has separately committed to identifying AI use on its charts and in its editorial coverage, while industry bodies are developing their own policies around whether fully AI-generated music should be eligible for certain charts. The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) and a group of major and independent music companies recently proposed principles that would keep fully AI-generated recordings off official charts unless certain conditions around authorisation, human contribution and fraud are met. Australia's ARIA Charts has also moved to exclude wholly AI-generated tracks from its charts and awards under its updated rules. So while Luminate's system isn't itself a chart-eligibility policy, it could provide an important piece of the infrastructure needed to enforce future rules. What does this mean for independent artists? For independent musicians, the most important takeaway isn't necessarily that AI-generated music is about to be banned or pushed out of streaming. It's that transparency is becoming increasingly important. If you're using AI tools as part of your creative process, make sure you understand the terms attached to those tools. Check what commercial rights you receive, whether the service allows distribution and whether you need to disclose AI involvement. It's also worth keeping records of your creative process. That might include project files, stems, songwriting notes, original recordings and information about which tools were used during production. You may never need to provide that information. But if a track is incorrectly flagged as AI-generated, having evidence of your creative process could become useful. Luminate says flagged content will have a dedicated review process, allowing artists and labels to respond if they believe an AI classification is incorrect. That's particularly important as automated identification systems become more widespread. AI detection won't be perfect No identification system is likely to get everything right. Luminate itself acknowledges that its database hasn't been fully processed and that some AI-generated content may not yet receive a label. The company says it is continuing to expand its coverage. For artists, that means an AI label shouldn't necessarily be treated as an absolute statement about how a track was created. There will inevitably be false positives, missed detections and grey areas. That's why Luminate's review process is potentially important. As these systems become more influential, artists need a way to challenge incorrect classifications rather than simply accepting an automated decision. The bigger issue, music discovery is getting noisier Perhaps the biggest reason this matters for independent artists is the effect AI could have on music discovery. Streaming platforms already contain enormous catalogues. Every day, thousands of new tracks compete for attention. Now add tens of thousands of AI-generated tracks to that ecosystem. The challenge isn't simply that AI music exists. It's that a huge increase in supply can make it harder for listeners to find the music created by artists they genuinely want to follow. That's why we're likely to see more sophisticated filtering, recommendation systems and transparency tools. For independent artists, this makes artist identity more valuable. A listener who discovers you isn't just choosing one song. They're potentially choosing an artist to follow, a catalogue to explore and a story to become invested in. That human connection is something a label on a database can't create for you. What artists should do now There's no need to panic about Luminate's announcement. Instead, use it as a reminder to get your digital music strategy in order. If you're releasing music independently, make sure your metadata is accurate and that your artist name, credits, ISRCs and release information are consistent across platforms. If you use AI during production, understand exactly what your chosen tools allow you to do commercially. Don't assume that being able to generate or download a track automatically means you have unrestricted rights to distribute it. And if you're creating predominantly human-made music, keep evidence of your creative process where practical. Most importantly, keep building your artist identity. Your music, social presence, live performances, collaborations and relationship with your audience all help distinguish your project from the enormous volume of content now entering streaming services. Distribution is only part of that process, but it's an important one. RouteNote gives independent artists and labels a way to distribute their music across major streaming and social platforms while maintaining control over their releases. As AI changes the volume and visibility of music online, having a clear release strategy, and making sure your catalogue is properly managed, will only become more important. A new standard for AI music transparency? Luminate describes its new framework as a starting point, rather than a finished solution. That's probably the most sensible way to look at it. The music industry is still figuring out how AI should be identified, labelled, measured and regulated. Streaming platforms are developing their own systems, AI companies are negotiating licensing arrangements and chart organisations are introducing new eligibility requirements. There isn't one universal standard yet. But Luminate's involvement is significant because CONNECT sits so close to the data infrastructure used by the wider music industry. If Luminate can combine its own identification technology with data from DSPs and AI music companies, it could eventually give labels, publishers, managers and artists a much clearer understanding of where AI-generated music is appearing and how it is performing. For independent artists, the message is simple: AI isn't just changing how music can be made. It's changing how music is identified, measured and understood. And as that system develops, staying informed about the rules could become just as important as staying creative. Distribute your music for FREE with RouteNote! content: BBC Introducing is expanding its support for emerging artists with a month-long series of live events across the UK this November, following the removal of its long-running stage from Reading & Leeds Festival. BBC Introducing is giving emerging artists a new reason to get their live sets ready, announcing a major programme of events taking place across the UK throughout November 2026. The month-long Introducing LIVE programme will visit 10 locations, bringing together live performances, workshops, open mic sessions, educational panels and networking opportunities for up-and-coming musicians, DJs and music creators. The announcement comes shortly after the BBC Introducing Stage was removed from this year's Reading & Leeds Festival after 18 years. For independent artists, the new programme could provide an important alternative route to live exposure at a time when opportunities for emerging musicians are increasingly valuable. BBC Introducing takes its live support on the road Introducing LIVE will take place across Belfast, Bridgend, Gateshead, Glasgow, Leeds, Liverpool, London, Manchester, Nottingham and Sunderland throughout November. The programme begins on November 5 with events in Bridgend and London before continuing around the UK. The month will finish with four special showcases in Leeds on November 28. Alongside performances, the programme will feature industry-focused activities designed to help artists develop their careers, including workshops, panels, open mics and networking opportunities. There will also be a songwriting camp in Manchester and a takeover event at The Fire Station in Sunderland, which will feature panels, workshops, open mic sessions and an industry feedback centre. BBC Introducing editor Kelly Betts said that championing and nurturing artists and creatives remains at the heart of the platform, describing this year's Introducing LIVE as its biggest edition yet. For artists still finding their feet in the industry, that combination of performance and education could be just as useful as the chance to get on stage. The announcement follows the removal of BBC Introducing from Reading & Leeds The new programme arrives at an interesting moment for BBC Introducing. In July, it was confirmed that the BBC Introducing Stage would no longer appear at Reading & Leeds Festival, ending an 18-year run at the event. Since launching in 2008, the stage had become one of the festival circuit's best-known platforms for emerging talent. Artists including Ed Sheeran and The 1975 played the stage early in their careers, while the BBC said around 70% of British artists on the 2026 Reading & Leeds lineup had previously been supported by BBC Introducing. The removal wasn't presented as an end to emerging-artist support at the festival. Festival Republic said its new Canopy stage would provide a platform for a wider pool of up-and-coming artists, with organisers arguing that opening the stage beyond BBC-selected acts could create opportunities for a more diverse range of new musicians. BBC Introducing also confirmed that it would continue working with other festivals, including The Great Escape and Latitude, to support emerging artists. Why live opportunities matter for independent artists For an independent musician, getting discovered online is only part of the equation. Streaming platforms can help listeners find new music, while social media allows artists to build audiences directly. But live performance offers something different: a direct connection between artist and audience. A strong festival performance can introduce an artist to hundreds of people in a single afternoon. It can also create opportunities to meet promoters, other musicians, managers, photographers and industry professionals. That's particularly important for artists who are still building their careers. A festival slot isn't necessarily going to result in an overnight breakthrough. But it can provide footage for social media, photographs for an EPK, new followers, future bookings and a chance to demonstrate that an artist can perform confidently in front of a crowd. The BBC Introducing model has historically been built around this combination of discovery and development, rather than simply putting new artists on a stage and sending them on their way. It's more than just a gig One of the most useful aspects of Introducing LIVE for emerging artists is the wider programme surrounding the performances. Workshops and educational panels can give musicians access to information that isn't always easy to find when you're working independently. Networking events can also provide an opportunity to meet people who could become collaborators or industry contacts further down the line. For newer artists, simply being in a room with other musicians and people working in the industry can be valuable. The live music industry can sometimes feel difficult to break into from the outside. Events that bring artists and industry professionals together can help make those connections more accessible. A reminder to independent artists, keep building your live profile The BBC Introducing announcement also highlights the importance of being ready when opportunities appear. If you're hoping to play festivals, showcases or support slots, having a professional live setup and a clear artist profile can make a difference. That means having your strongest songs ready, an up-to-date EPK, good-quality live footage and a clear online presence. It also means making sure your recorded music is easy to find when someone discovers you after a show. For independent artists using digital distribution, keeping your catalogue organised across major streaming platforms is another important part of that process. A new listener who discovers you at a live event should be able to search your name and immediately find your latest music. Platforms such as RouteNote allow independent artists and labels to distribute their music across major streaming and social platforms, helping turn those real-world discoveries into longer-term listeners. BBC Introducing remains an important route for new music Despite the change at Reading & Leeds, the latest announcement suggests BBC Introducing isn't stepping back from emerging artists. If anything, it is taking a broader approach. Rather than concentrating its live activity around one major festival stage, Introducing LIVE will bring opportunities to artists in cities across the UK. That geographical spread could be particularly valuable for musicians outside London's traditional industry hubs. And that matters. The UK has a huge community of independent artists creating music outside the biggest cities and established industry networks. Bringing workshops, performances and networking events to places such as Sunderland, Gateshead, Bridgend and Belfast creates more opportunities for artists to participate without necessarily having to travel to London. For musicians trying to build a career from the ground up, accessibility can make a real difference. What should artists do next? If you're an emerging artist, it's worth keeping an eye on BBC Introducing's upcoming opportunities and making sure your artist profile is ready for them. But don't wait for one particular festival or showcase to validate your project. Keep releasing music. Keep performing wherever you can. Build relationships with local venues and other artists. Capture your live performances and use that material to strengthen your online presence. And when an opportunity like Introducing LIVE comes along, you'll be in a much stronger position to take advantage of it. The removal of BBC Introducing from Reading & Leeds might have closed one door for emerging artists, but this new programme suggests the organisation is keen to open several more. content: As orchestras take on more and more popular applications, producers may often want to work with the real thing instead of using sample packs. Japan’s Dreamtonics is working to close that gap with Instrument X. This plugin uses AI to control the human elements of playing orchestral instruments such as breath pressure and bow friction, adding a more dynamic contrast than adjusting volume or applying stock effects. Dreamtonics calls the process “Neural Acoustics Modelling”. Beyond individual adjustments to the playing style, Instrument X also employs “3D Sound-Field Control.” This function allows instruments to be placed in mockups of different microphone configurations, such as spot, Decca Tree, and ambient pairs. The technology alters the sound waves themselves with the different notation options instead of triggering different static audio files. Moreover, the UI is modelled after standard DAWs, making the workflow transition seamless. The new adjustment options are simply parameters to experiment with. Dreamtonics has released 11 different packs related to Instrument X. There is the free standalone version and DAW plugin, and the other 10 range from $99 to $649, offering Instrument X with software instruments, software instrument packs on their own, and a complete collection. content: Arrangement is one of the most important parts of music production. It's how every artist fits their sounds together into one cohesive piece of music. And LA-based music education brand Color With Live has developed a new tool, Stencils, which helps users master the concept of arrangement. Imagine having access to the Ableton project of a Skrillex song. All the tracks are laid out for the drums, vocals, bass, etc, and all the clips are in the arrangement view. With a stencil, the key difference is that there are no sounds in the clips. You get to fill in the sounds yourself, like a colouring book for Ableton. READ MORE: Core Sampler is “the sampler Pro Tools should already have” – this is how it works This creates room for experimentation. Simply put your chosen sounds in the associated clips, follow the instructions, such as when to cut the low frequencies, and the final product will be a complete song because the arrangement is based on a track that’s worked on dancefloors around the world. Each stencil also clearly labels drops, breakdowns, and other sections to help users get a feel for what each part looks like in a session. “Producers download Serum packs to practice sound design and MIDI packs to practice music theory. We were blown away that nothing like that existed for arrangement. The advice is always to pick apart your reference tracks, but there's nothing visual to check your work," says Kevin Rea, co-founder of Colour With Live. “Our mission isn’t for our stencil to be a crutch that you rely on for every song, but instead something that you can learn from and then apply to future productions.” Rea and his fellow co-founder, Grant Hunter, came up with the idea for Stencils because, like many young producers, they have to work full-time on top of working on their music. After coming home from a long day, they wouldn’t know where to start when they were staring at an empty Ableton window. Stencils allowed them to get their creativity flowing and finish songs. Now, they have created over 250 Stencils in a variety of genres such as UK Garage, Dubstep, Tech House, Drum & Bass, Techno, and Hip-Hop. For a limited time, they are offering a free pack of three Stencils based on Flip It by Levity, Fisher’s rework of World Hold On by Bob Sinclar, and Dimension’s Once In A Lifetime. View the full stencil library and learn more at Color With Live. content: Every week, we round up the most exciting new plugin releases — from virtual instruments and creative effects to mixing tools and workflow upgrades. There are tons of plugins released every week, both free and paid-for, so be sure to check back here every Friday to find out the software worth adding to your plugin folder. This week’s new and noteworthy virtual instruments, effects and mixing plugins [Updated 27 August 2026] Dawesome – Abyss 2 Dawesome has released Abyss 2, the next evolution of its unique cinematic synthesizer where patches are created by placing ‘tone colours’ on a visual gradient to shape the sound by both ear and eye. The update adds a new timbral extraction engine, where users can drop in any sound and Abyss will reconstruct it as a ‘palette’ of tone colours, automatically tuned and ready to play. Other highlights in Abyss 2 include a polyrhythmic sequencer, a new effects chain with four slots and 20 effects to populate them, various workflow improvements, and over 200 new presets. Abyss 2 is available from Dawesome for intro pricing of £69 (full price £119), or existing owners can upgrade for £35 (full price £60). Cherry Audio – Memorymode 2 It seems to be the week for sequels, with Cherry Audio releasing a major update to Memorymode, significantly expanding the capabilities of its Memorymoog-inspired polysynth plugin. According to the developer, its analogue modelling has been significantly improved using cutting-edge analysis and emulation techniques, delivering more accurate oscillators, filters, and envelopes. The effects section has been upgraded with three independent effects chains and 22 studio-quality effects, including the new Wide Phaser and Rotary Speaker. The Version 2 update also adds support for polyphonic aftertouch and MPE, letting users create more expressive patches, and the preset browser has been redesigned as well. Memorymode 2 is available from Cherry Audio for $69, with upgrade pricing available to existing owners when they log into their accounts. JMG Sound – Continuum JMG Sound has launched Continuum, a delay plugin inspired by the gritty imperfection of classic hardware units. It features two identical but independent delay engines, letting users mix and match from three models — Tape, BBD, and Digital — with a Mojo parameter for exaggerating the unique physical characteristics of each one. The signals of each can then be mixed using the Crossfeed controls, with a Diffuse control that uses all-pass filters to smear the edges into blooming, reverb-like spaces that can be further tailored with modulation and damping. Users can also set their delay repeats to follow organic, humanlike grooves and syncopation. Need somewhere to start? Use the intelligent randomisation button. Continuum is available from United Plugins for intro pricing of £13 (full price £68). Sonible – Smart:chain Sonible has launched Smart:chain, described by the developer as ‘the intelligent channel strip’. It combines EQ, compression, de-harshing, gating, input riding, saturation, and leveling, all within one intelligent, AI-assisted plugin. According to Sonible, Smart:chain’s processors can analyse your audio and interact to create a coherent processing chain, rather than operating independently. As each plugin instance can communicate with the others across your session, it’s easy to manage tracks within the context of the entire mix using smart depth staging, and you can even access every Smart:chain instance in a single window. Smart:chain is available from Sonible for intro pricing of £85 (full price £149), and there’s a 40% education discount available for students and teachers too. Codwaves – BassXtend Closing this week’s round-up is another mix tool, this time from Codwaves. Named BassXtend, the plugin is designed to make 808s, synth and bass guitar, and kicks more perceptible on phones, earbuds, and laptops. How does it do it? It generates harmonics based on the pitch of the incoming signal, and the ear reconstructs the fundamental frequency, even though it can’t be reproduced on smaller speaker drivers. BassXtend offers four simple controls: Intensity, Root (which acts as the crossover point), gain trim, and Low Band In/Out. Crucially, it only generates harmonics above the crossover point you set, so it won’t add headroom-eating low frequency content. BassXtend is available from Codwaves for intro pricing of £9 (full price £14). Where to download free plugins and VSTs Looking for free plugins? Our freeware section is an excellent place to start; each month, we also compile round-ups of the best free plugins and samples to download. The production community is full of passionate developers who’ve given away instruments, effects and other plugins as freeware. Some of our favourites include Valhalla’s Supermassive reverb and Matt Tytel’s Helm polysynth. Remember, most developers also offer free trials for their plugins. How to Book Your Own Shows in 2026 (Without a Booking Agent) Why Booking Gigs Without an Agent Feels So Hard The wall most artists hit isn't effort. It's information. To book a show, you need three things: venues that fit your size and genre, the name of the person who actually books the room, and a few comparable artists you can point to as proof you belong on that bill. The problem is that most venues never publish their talent buyer's contact. What sits on the website is a general inbox that whoever's around checks between shifts, not the person making decisions. That gap is what has kept independent artists stuck for years. The good news: closing it is a skill you can learn. How to Find Venues for Music That Fit You Before you email anyone, build a realistic target list. Pitching 1,000-cap rooms while you're drawing 15 people gets you ignored, and it burns rooms you might be right for in a year. The smarter move is to look at where similar-sized artists already play and work backward from there. Name similar artists: Write down 10 to 20 artists whose sound and audience are close to yours. Follow their live show history: The rooms that book artists at your level have already shown they'll take that chance. Those are your first targets. Pitch yourself to these venues: Find the right talent buyer for the venue and reach out to pitch yourself for an upcoming show! Booking-Agent.io was built for exactly this, and it works the opposite way from a venue directory. A directory is a static roster you scroll, built for a different tier of act and updated on someone else's schedule. Booking-Agent.io is a real-time search engine: type in a similar artist and it pulls the venues, promoters, and talent buyers tied to that artist's actual performance history, so the contacts reflect who's booking at your level right now instead of who booked two years ago. You can also search by city and by genre when you're zeroing in on a market. That similar-artist search is the part most booking tools simply do not have. Genre and city filters get you a list; starting from a comparable act gets you the rooms that already book your sound. See it in action in this quick walkthrough: How to Reach the Talent Buyer, Not the General Inbox A talent buyer is the person at a venue or promoter who decides which artists get booked and on which nights. They are the ones who actually say yes, and the address on a venue's website is rarely how you reach them. Promoters often rent the room themselves and carry the risk, and like talent buyers, they rarely post their direct contact anywhere public. That's the point where most DIY booking quietly stalls. Booking-Agent.io finds and verifies the talent buyer and promoter behind each room, rather than handing you a prebuilt list someone bought once and let go stale, so your pitch reaches the person who can green-light the show instead of a shared inbox. NOTE: You unlock contacts with credits, and a credit is only spent when a verified email is actually found. Searching venues is free, and a search that turns up nothing costs you nothing. That isn't the norm in this category, so it's worth knowing before you start. How to Route a Tour That Doesn't Lose Money Even a three-city run lives or dies on routing. Margins are thin at the independent level, and every empty drive between cities you couldn't book eats into them. Cluster your dates. Keep shows close enough that you're not driving six hours between them. Fill the gaps on purpose. Locked Chicago and need a stop on the way to Nashville? Pull the artists who play that corridor and see who's booking there, instead of guessing. Use the map. Booking-Agent.io plots venues geographically, so routing corridors and open gaps are easy to spot at a glance. Save data when you're ready. Save your venue and contact lists to plan the rest of your routing, which helps if you're a manager juggling several artists or a label lining up release-timed dates, shows, and tours. If you're timing a run to build buzz in each market, pairing your dates with local radio play compounds the effect. How to Organize Your Outreach So Nothing Slips The usual mistake is treating booking like one big sprint: fire off a batch of emails, follow up once, move on. The artists who get traction treat it like a pipeline. Group your venues by tour leg (a regional run, a festival cycle, a single market) and track every conversation on its own. Booking-Agent.io lets you save venues into named Projects, so a "US Tour 2026" list stays separate from a "UK Run, Fall" list, and each artist on your roster gets their own. It sounds like a small thing. In practice, it's the difference between real momentum and a pile of emails nobody answered. What to Say When You Reach Out Your first email to a talent buyer should be short and specific. They hear from a lot of artists, and the ones who stand out lead with context instead of hype. Reference a similar act. "I saw you've booked [Artist X] a few times. We get compared to them a lot and just wrapped a run in [market]." That puts credibility and fit in one line. Be honest about your draw. If you have a number, use it. If you don't, say where you are and where you're headed. Buyers respect artists who know their own level. Make the ask clear. Headlining a small room, opening for someone, taking a late slot? Say which one. "I'd love to play sometime" is a wish, not a request. Send a link, not a file. A Spotify link, a recent live clip, a short EPK. Not a 4MB attachment nobody opens. One habit keeps you professional and out of spam folders: reach out to people one at a time, say who you are, and drop anyone the second they ask off your list. If you're emailing venues in another country, take a minute to check that market's outreach rules. A real-time tool like Booking-Agent.io does that research in minutes by pulling venues and verified talent buyer contacts from a similar artist's live history. Is Booking-Agent.io a good Sonicbids alternative for booking your own shows? They solve different halves of the problem, so the honest answer is that it depends on what you need. Sonicbids is best known as an electronic press kit tool, great for packaging your bio, music, and photos into one link. Booking-Agent.io starts a step earlier, at the question of who to send that press kit to: type in an artist you sound like, and it returns the venues, promoters, and verified talent buyers tied to that artist's real performance history. Many artists use an EPK tool to build the pitch and Booking-Agent.io to find the right person to send it to. What is the best alternative to a venue directory like Pollstar or Gigwell for independent artists? Industry directories are excellent if you are an agency that needs a broad standing reference and has the budget for it. For an independent artist booking their own run, the gap is that a directory tells you a venue exists, not who is booking it right now or which rooms actually fit your draw. It varies, but most work on commission, commonly 10 percent and sometimes up to 15 percent. It's real, ongoing work, which is exactly why they wait for artists who can already fill a room. How far ahead should you book? It depends on the room and the market, but reaching out well before your target date and keeping your dates geographically close gives you the best shot at a clean, profitable run. content: EQ, or equalization, is a tool that allows us to control and modify the tonal makeup of audio. This is useful to correct imperfections and to enhance certain tonal characteristics while reducing others. How does EQ work? EQ tools work by boosting or cutting the amplitude (i.e, volume) of specific frequencies within a sound. EQ processors typically include multiple ‘bands’. Each band operates around a specific frequency, and different types of band will affect the surrounding frequencies in different ways. What are the different types of EQ band? Credit: Minimal Audio Parametric / Peak: Creates a bell- or trough-like curve centred on the band’s frequency. The width of the curve is controlled by the “Q” or “Bandwidth” setting. Low Shelving: Progressively cuts or boosts frequencies that lie below the band’s frequency. Typically, some frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency will also be affected High Shelving: The functional opposite of a low shelving band. Impacts frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency. Low Cut: A low cut band is the same as a high-pass filter, and so blocks frequencies that fall below the band’s frequency. High Cut: A high cut band is the same as a low-pass filter, and so blocks frequencies that lie above the band’s frequency. It is the functional opposite of a low cut filter. What are the different types of EQ processor? EQ plugins and processors usually combine multiple types of bands into a single unit. These are the three most common varieties: Studio- or console-style EQ: Typically combines a low-shelving and high-shelving band with two parametric bands. Sometimes also includes low- and high-cut bands. Pultec-style EQ: Based on vintage outboard EQ processors. Typically handles cutting and boosting as separate bands. Band frequency selection is usually stepped rather than continuous. Graphic EQ: Combines a number of fixed-frequency, fixed-width peak bands. Band boost/cut is controlled by a fader. The pattern of faders creates a graphical curve, hence “graphic” EQ. When should I use EQ? EQ is used extensively at all stages in the recording process. Input conditioning: Hardware EQs and preamps/recording channels that include EQ are useful for optimising the recorded sound, countering mic colouration, and correcting obvious problems. Tracking: Use temporary EQ during tracking to create a comfortable working mix. Also use on cue mixes to enhance/reduce prominence of elements the performer needs to hear more/less clearly. Mixing: Use to sculpt and shape the frequencies of your parts to give each its own spectral space within the mix, and to help bring the parts together into a cohesive whole. Mastering: Use tightly-focused / high-Q EQ to fix specific frequency issues; use broad low-Q EQ to make gentle changes to the overall tonal balance. Which EQs should you use? All DAWs come with at least one type of EQ plugin, and often include multiple varieties. You're certainly able to garner pro-grade results with the EQs in your DAW, or any free EQs that are out there. However, if you're looking for an EQ with expanded features, a different interface, or would like an emulation of a classic hardware EQ, you might want to look around the third-party plugin marketplace. content: 60 years ago, Jimi Hendrix first plugged in and played through a Marshall amplifier – and it was the start of a true musical love affair. Instantly, Marshall amps became a key component in Hendrix’s legendary guitar tones. To honour its Hendrix’s relationship with Marshall amps, the brand is releasing the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Collection. Over the year, Marshall has released a slew of guitar gear, including the 1959 JMH Half Stack inspired by Hendrix’s own rig and limited-edition Fuzz Face pedal. But Marshall has left the best ‘til last; the Anniversary collection is gaining three new additions, in the form of sleek new headphones, a speaker, and a new hand-made amplifier inspired by the iconic Studio Vintage amp. READ MORE: “For him, reverb was green, distortion was red”: Eddie Kramer on Jimi Hendrix seeing effects in music as colours First up, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Major V headphones will allow fans to listen to Hendrix classics on the go. With a foldable design, the headphones are perfect to pop in your bag but still pack a crisp, Marshall-standard listening experience. If you’re keen to share your Hendrix listening experience with others, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Emberton III might be up your alley. Complete with the collection’s signature cosmic, purple design, with a silver all-seeing eye on the media jog and purple LEDs. Each silicon sleeve is also unique, due to them all being hand-dipped in a water transfer print. Credit: Marshall Now for the pièce de résistance – the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition JMH Studio Bundle. The hand-made from quality plywood and wrapped in black Tolex, the amp is based on the classic Studio Vintage amp and promises to provide “expressive cleans and deep blues textures”. The 20W valve head comes with power reduction to 5W, two bridgeable channels as well as two ECC83 preamp valves, an ECC83 phase splitter, and two EL34 power valves There’s also a switchable series effects loop. The amp also wears a comic-inspired black and purple psychedelic pattern across its control panel alongside purple LEDs. Silver beading is also across the entire amp, with Hendrix’s beloved all-seeing eye motif also sitting on the top and bottom of the stack. Credit: Marshall “The story of Jimi and Marshall has always been personal to me because I first heard it from my dad, Al Hendrix,” Hendrix’s sister, Janie Hendrix, explains. “Dad was there and shared those memories with me, so I carry that story only one degree from its source.” “Jimi was always searching for a sound that did not yet exist, pushing beyond what anyone thought an electric guitar could do,” she continues. “Marshall gave him the power and freedom to turn those bold ideas into a sound the world had never heard before. Sixty years later, that connection between Jimi and Marshall still speaks to new generations of musicians who are pushing creative boundaries and searching for their own sound.” In terms of other artists searching for their own sound, American blues-rock artist Ally Venable had the honour of trying out the new Marshall Studio Vintage JMH before anyone else. As she experiments with her tone on the new bit of kit, she explains just how Hendrix and Marshall shaped her musical journey. In terms of pricing, the Hendrix 60th Anniversary Edition Major V headphones will set you back £129.99. As for the speaker, the Emberton III costs £149.99, while the JMH Studio Bundle amp is £1,749.99. In terms of Hendrix, rare new footage of Jimi Hendrix’s legendary 1969 Woodstock show has also recently surfaced online. Captured by a student who snuck onstage, the hour-and-a-half video gives an entirely new perspective on the legendary show. The collection is available to order from 25 August, with retail availability beginning 9 September 2026. For more information, head to Marshall. content: This article was originally published October 15, 2025 and updated Monday, August 24, 2026. In the lead-up to a release, a strong promo strategy can help build anticipation and drive early fan engagement. But here’s the problem: without a follow-up release, tour, or campaign, excitement builds and peaks on release day, then quickly fades. It’s a cycle independent artists endure, but it doesn’t build a fanbase. That’s where a waterfall release strategy helps. Instead of releasing a full album all at once, you roll it out gradually through single releases. This keeps fans coming back, helps you reach new listeners, and gives each track from your larger project more room to shine. In this blog, you’ll learn how to set up a waterfall release and use it to boost streams, deepen fan relationships, and get more long-term value from your music. What is a waterfall release strategy? A waterfall release strategy allows you to release an album or EP in increments, releasing individual singles that you can stack to direct traffic back to previous releases. In simple terms, the waterfall approach is: Release a single ahead of the album release Release a second single, including the first single in this release, too Release a third single with the two prior singles, and so on… Why should I use a waterfall release strategy? Waterfall releases help you build anticipation and momentum ahead of a full project, boosting streams by promoting each track individually over time—rather than all at once. This approach has many benefits for independent artists looking to get the most out of their full-length releases. Extend the lifespan of your release: Turn each track into a mini-campaign to keep momentum going. Maximize playlist opportunities: Releasing separate singles allows you to pitch each on to Spotify Editorial playlists and maximize other playlist placements. Work with the algorithm: Steady, spaced out releases drive consistent engagement which platform algorithms reward. Attract new listeners: Singles are easy entry points for new listeners. Each release builds curiosity and draws fans deeper into your music. How do I use a waterfall release strategy? You can use the waterfall approach on your next release by following the steps below. The key to this approach is maintaining accurate ISRCs and metadata to allow streaming data to carry over on re-released tracks. 1. Choose your singles and prepare artwork for each release Identify a few tracks you want to release ahead of your album. Typically, artists release 3 singles that capture different sounds and themes from the longer-form work. The waterfall strategy requires new artwork for each release. Avoid using your intended ultimate album art for your singles as it will be unusable for your album without cancelling the prior release that uses it. 2. Choose a distributor CD Baby makes it easy to waterfall your release and get your music on over 150 streaming platforms worldwide. 3. Decide on a release schedule Once you’ve decided what singles you want to release and how you’ll distribute them, decide the order and timing of each single leading up to your album. It’s typical to give at least a month of space between releases to give each track sufficient time in the spotlight. 4. Submit your first single Submit your track through a distributor like CD Baby and follow your typical release strategy for a single, but boost anticipation by mentioning it’s a track off an upcoming full-length album. 5. Re-release your first single with a second single About a month after your first single, release a second single along with the first single, using the same ISRC for Single 1 to re-release, along with a new UPC and album artwork. If you’re distributing with CD Baby, note that our release creation process defines a single release as one track only, and an album release as two tracks or more. More information here. 6. Re-release your first and second singles with a third single After another month, release your first two singles with a new third single. Again, create new artwork and a UPC for the release, but use the same ISRCs for Singles 1 and 2 to carry over your streams. You can promote each of your singles as a standalone release, following our ultimate music release strategy guide for 2025 for best results. Important Reminder: Match your Metadata and ISRCs In order to carry over your streaming data every time you re-release a track, you must ensure the metadata and ISRC codes match the original track. Details on how to find your ISRCs here. Conclusion Ready to get started? Trusted by a growing community of over two million independent artists, CD Baby is with you every step of the way—from release to promotion—offering easy distribution to over 150 streaming platforms worldwide and marketing tools and insights to grow your fanbase. Get Started FAQs How do I pay for a waterfall release with CD Baby? The waterfall release is a strategy, not a CD Baby product. As such, you’ll need to purchase a separate submission for each release — from your first single to your final album. When the full album is ready to come out, can the track order be different from the waterfall order? Absolutely. Track order will always appear in the order you’ve entered for a release upon submitting it for distribution. How many singles should I waterfall before dropping a full album? You can release as many singles as you like before dropping a full album, but be aware that as track number or total runtime accumulate, digital streaming platforms might start showing releases as albums rather than singles. More information on how releases are categorized across platforms here. The post What is a waterfall release and how do I set one up? appeared first on DIY Musician.

content: As of August 2026, AI music policies are changing fast. This article reflects the latest guidance available at the time of writing, but creators should always review current platform, distributor, and tool-specific terms before submitting a release. Whether you like it or not, AI is here. In the music industry, artists are using AI tools to make demos, test song ideas, generate vocals, create cover art, build music videos, and in some cases, create full tracks from scratch. But there’s a big difference between using AI as part of your creative process and using AI to copy another artist, impersonate a real person, mislead listeners, or flood DSPs with low-effort uploads. At Symphonic, we believe there is a responsibility to support creators who are experimenting with new tools while still protecting artists, rights holders, platforms, and fans from misuse. We believe the problem starts when AI is used in ways that create confusion around rights, ownership, identity, or intent. If a track was made with AI, that needs to be disclosed. If you upload something, you need to know where it came from, what tool made it, and what that tool actually allows you to do with the final track. If the release imitates someone else, misrepresents what it is, or tries to game the system, that crosses a line… Although the rules around AI music are still changing, a few things are clear. If you’re thinking of submitting any AI-assisted or AI-generated music, here’s how to do it responsibly. AI Music Distribution in 2026: What Artists Need to Know Before Releasing Anything Be Clear About How AI Was Used Before you submit a release, be honest about where AI showed up in the process. Was it part of the audio? The artwork? The video? Did it help shape the writing, production, vocals, or final master? Did it generate the entire track? Someone could’ve used AI to generate a quick melody idea, then rewrote and recorded the full song themselves. Another artist might’ve used AI to create cover art. Someone else might’ve used a platform like Suno to generate most of the audio. Those are all very different situations. How AI was used affects what you might need to disclose, what terms you should review, and how the release may be handled by different platforms or partners. That’s why it’s important to know exactly how AI was used before you submit anything for distribution. The main thing is to be clear about what YOU actually made. If AI helped create part of the final release, be honest about that. Know exactly what tool you used, what it generated, and how that output ended up in the finished product. When distributing through Symphonic, you’ll need to disclose these details so the release can be reviewed and delivered responsibly based on how AI was used and what each DSP currently requires. How To Know If You're Allowed to Distribute What You Made Before you submit AI-related music, separate three questions: How was the track made? Was AI used for a prompt, a demo, a vocal, a stem, a master, the artwork, the video, or the full recording? Do you have the rights needed to distribute it? Did the AI platform give you the right to commercially use the output? Did you upload anything into the tool that you don’t fully own or have permission to use? Will every DSP, monetization tool, or rights management program treat it the same way? Not always. A release may be distributable in one context but still face extra review, disclosure requirements, promotion limits, monetization restrictions, or platform-specific rules somewhere else. Start by checking the terms of the AI platform you used. Look for anything that explains: Commercial use Ownership Monetization Licensing Prohibited uses User-generated content Download rules Plan-specific rights Those sections usually tell you what you can and can’t do with the audio, artwork, lyrics, vocals, or video the tool helped create. Pay attention to the plan you were on when you made it, the date you created or downloaded the content, and the current terms tied to that output. Some platforms treat free users, paid users, and enterprise users differently, and those terms can change over time. A paid subscription also doesn’t automatically mean every release is cleared for every type of distribution, monetization, or platform use. Suno’s recent Terms update is a good example of why this matters. Its new Terms of Service take effect September 3, 2026, and Suno has said the update will clarify rights around user content, commercial use, and downloads. That doesn’t mean every creator’s situation is identical. It means artists need to check the plan they used, when the content was created or downloaded, and what the current terms actually allow before assuming something is safe to release. Look at what you put into the tool. Ask yourself: Did I upload samples, stems, vocals, lyrics, artwork, or another artist’s song as a reference? Did I use anything I don’t fully own or have permission to use? Did my prompt ask for something that sounds like a real artist, brand, or specific copyrighted work? If the input creates a rights problem, the output will probably create one too. Keep a simple record of what you used and when. Save the platform name, the date you created the content, the date you downloaded it, the account or plan you used, and any terms tied to that output. Screenshotting the relevant terms can also help just in case they change later. If you can’t clearly explain where the content came from, what tool helped make it, and what that tool allows you to do with it, don’t submit the release until you can. Do Not Use AI to Copy, Impersonate, or Mislead AI can be part of your creative process, but it shouldn’t be used to fake, copy, or confuse people. That’s where responsible use turns into misuse. Symphonic does not allow content that clearly infringes on existing copyrighted works, intentionally mimics or impersonates real artists, brands, or individuals without authorization, or uses misleading metadata. We also don’t allow spam, mass-generated low-quality uploads, or attempts to manipulate DSPs. In simple terms: don’t use AI to make people think they’re hearing someone they’re not. Don’t title, tag, or package a release in a way that misleads listeners or platforms. Don’t use AI to flood stores with low-effort tracks just to chase streams. If the release depends on confusing people to work, it’s not something you should be submitting. Not Every Platform Treats AI Music the Same Way DSPs, platforms, and monetization programs all have different rules around AI-generated or AI-assisted content. A release can be okay for one DSP and still need extra review, disclosure, or restrictions somewhere else. For example, right now: Audible Magic, Meta, Bandcamp, and YouTube Content ID do not accept works created with generative AI. Apple Music and Vevo require AI disclosure for music videos if AI was used in the creation of the video. Spotify has announced AI Persona badges for artist profiles that represent AI-generated artist identities rather than real people. Starting in mid-September 2026, music from AI Personas generally will not be included in Spotify’s editorial or algorithmic recommendations by default, unless listeners show intentional engagement signals like following the AI Persona artist. Some monetization and rights management tools may have stricter requirements than standard distribution, especially when the release involves fully AI-generated audio, AI-generated vocals, or unclear rights. That Spotify update is important because AI disclosure is no longer just an administrative step. It can affect how a release or artist profile is surfaced, recommended, promoted, and monetized. Using AI as a creative tool is one thing. Building a public artist identity around an AI-generated persona is another, and platforms are starting to treat those situations differently. If those details are missing or wrong, your release can get held up, blocked from certain platforms, or lose access to monetization tools you were counting on. In some cases, it can create problems after delivery too, meaning something you thought was already live and handled may need to be reviewed, corrected, restricted, or taken down. Being upfront doesn’t mean every platform will accept the release, but hiding or leaving out AI details can definitely make things worse. Creators Should Have a Say in How Their Music Is Used by AI At Symphonic, we believe if an AI company wants to train on real music, creators should have a say in how their work is used, what permissions are attached to it, and whether they want to participate at all. That’s why we partnered with Sureel AI. Through this partnership, participating artists can opt in to fully licensed AI datasets instead of having their music used without permission or outside a clear licensing framework. For creators, this means if you want your music included in licensed AI datasets, there can be a path to do that where you can be fairly compensated. If you don’t, your work shouldn’t be treated like it’s automatically up for grabs just because it’s on the internet. “AI represents real opportunity for artists, but only if we use it correctly,” explains Jorge Brea, our Founder and CEO at Symphonic. “By giving our artists the chance to opt in to Sureel’s fully licensed AI datasets, we are pushing back against unpaid training and opening new revenue opportunities for those who wish to participate.” Questions to Ask Before You Submit AI-Related Music Before you submit an AI-assisted or AI-generated release, take a minute to check the basics. Ask yourself: Did AI help create the audio, artwork, video, lyrics, vocals, production, or final master? Did I disclose AI use where required? Do I know which platform or tool was used? Did I check the terms for that tool? Did I upload anything into the tool that I don’t fully own or have permission to use? Does the release imitate a real artist, voice, brand, or existing song? Am I trying to use AI to make something real, or am I flooding platforms with low-effort content? Am I expecting this release to qualify for every DSP, monetization tool, or rights management program? If any of those answers are unclear, don’t submit yet! Figure it out first. It’s better to fix the issue before delivery than to deal with the takedown, rejection, or blocked monetization after the release is already in motion. Protect Your Music Before It Gets Misused AI doesn’t only affect the music you’re making next… It can also affect the music, vocals, and catalog you’ve already released. At a recent conference we attended, there was an artist speaking about how their voice was used without their consent, and their work was used in ways they never agreed to, by people they’ve never even heard of. As a company run by musicians, this is something that we personally feel for. The idea that someone can take your voice, your sound, or your catalog and use it without permission is unsettling, especially when it feels like there’s nothing you can do about it… That’s one of the reasons we’re happy to have recently partnered with ArtyShield, the AI trust infrastructure platform built to help artists, labels, vocalists, and rights holders protect their music and voices from unauthorized AI use. Through this partnership, Symphonic clients can access tools like: MusicShield, which helps protect tracks from being used to train AI models without consent while keeping the audio quality intact. VoiceShield, which helps protect vocal performances from unauthorized cloning, synthesis, and synthetic voice misuse. We aren’t fully anti-AI. We just strongly believe artists should have real tools to protect their work, their voice, and their identity as this technology keeps evolving. Symphonic clients can now access ArtyShield directly through the Client Offerings section in SymphonicMS. Getting started is free, with paid tiers available for clients who need deeper protection and expanded access to ArtyShield’s tools. Ready to try it out? Log in to your SymphonicMS account to check it out today. Final Thoughts… AI is evolving fast, and the truth is, it’s going to bring both positives and negatives to the music industry. For artists, the goal isn’t to fear every new tool or jump into every trend without thinking. The goal is to stay informed and make sure the way you use AI still respects the people and work behind the music. At Symphonic, we believe there’s a future where AI can support creativity without replacing accountability. That future depends on transparency, permission, and giving creators the power to choose when they want to participate… and when they don’t. Here's everything you need to know before you go… Everything You Need To Know Before Attending BOmm When: September 8th - 11th, 2026 Where: Bogotá, Colombia About BOmm The Bogotá Music Market (BOmm) is one of the biggest meet-ups for Colombia’s music industry, bringing artists, managers, labels, booking agents, distributors, and industry pros together in the heart of Bogotá. Organized by the Bogotá Chamber of Commerce, BOmm is more than panels and showcases. It’s a space to network, discover new talent, build business opportunities, and get a real pulse on where the music industry is headed across Latin America and beyond. Now in its 15th edition, BOmm continues to be a key market for artists and music professionals looking to make real connections, share ideas, and expand into new territories. For 2026, BOmm is also opening its call to international artists for the first time, creating even more opportunities for cross-border exchange and collaboration. At this conference, you’ll experience things like: Conference Programming: Talks, workshops, conversations, and sessions with music industry leaders covering the trends, challenges, and opportunities shaping the business today. Showcases: Live performances from selected artists and bands, giving attendees the chance to discover new talent from Colombia and beyond. BOmm Connect: One-on-one business meetings designed to help artists, managers, agencies, labels, and other music professionals create new opportunities, partnerships, and deals. Networking: Dedicated spaces to meet other professionals, broaden your contacts, connect with people working across the same side of the business, and build strategic relationships. Noches BOmm: Extended programming that keeps the energy going beyond the daytime conference schedule. Tips For Visiting Bogotá Bogotá is situated at a high altitude (around 2,600 meters or 8,500 feet above sea level). If you're not accustomed to high altitudes, take it easy for the first day or two to acclimate to the thinner air. Bogotá's weather can be very unpredictable, so prepare for anything from sudden temperature changes to occasional rain. While public transportation in Bogotá is improving, we recommend using secure transportation options like official taxis or ride-hailing services (You can either call one or use apps such as Tappsi and EasyTaxi). No matter what, always avoid unmarked taxis. Last but not least, eat all the delicious food your heart desires. (Especially some Ajiaco, Arepas, Pan de Bono, and so much more…) Janette Berrios, VP of Corporate Marketing at Symphonic, will be speaking on a panel, “Digital Strategies: How to Create a Marketing Plan for Your Music”. content: The music industry has changed a lot over the years, but for some reason, there are still some persistent myths that keep getting passed around like it's 2008. Things like needing a label to make it as an artist, that getting playlisted will save your release, going viral means you made it… the list goes on and on. The problem is, a lot of these ideas sound believable because sometimes there is a little truth in them. Labels can help. Playlists can move the needle. Viral moments can open doors. But none of these things work the way people think they do, and treating them like some shortcut to fame and fortune can lead you in the wrong direction completely. We’re here to clear these up so you can change your perspective, make smarter decisions, and stop chasing career moves that no longer matter in 2026. Key Takeaways: Getting paid from music requires understanding which rights and revenue streams you actually control. Attention is not the same thing as a sustainable career. Ownership is more complicated than simply saying, “I own the song.” Artists make smarter decisions when they understand the business behind the music. Debunking 11 Common Music Industry Myths #1: “You need a record label to make it.” The truth: A label can help, but it’s not the only way to build a real career anymore. In 2026, you can upload a song worldwide, build a fanbase online, sell merch, book shows, run your own ads, collect analytics, and make money from multiple revenue streams without being signed. That’s not to say that labels are useless; a great label can absolutely help take something that already has momentum and make it into something bigger. But a deal won’t magically create a fanbase, fix weak branding, or turn a song with no strategy into a hit. Think of a label as a possible partner, not the prize. If you’re already gaining traction on your own, the right label can help with things like funding, marketing support, bigger campaign planning, playlist pitching, press, radio, sync opportunities, and connections you may not have access to yet. But if you’re not, a label deal won’t create that foundation for you. Focus on building the kind of momentum a partner can actually add to. The stronger your audience, catalog, and strategy are before a deal, the more useful the right label can be. #2: “Spotify only pays a few cents, so streaming doesn’t matter.” The truth: There isn’t one flat Spotify payout rate that applies to every artist, every stream, in every country. We hear it all the time: “Spotify only pays $0.003 per stream, so what’s even the point?” But in reality, that number is a rough average people repeat online, not some guaranteed rate. Spotify actually pays based on something called streamshare, which means payouts are calculated from a royalty pool and divided based on each rights holder’s share of total streams. That doesn’t mean concerns about low streaming payouts aren’t valid. They are. But writing off streaming completely misses the bigger picture. I get it, streams alone probably won’t build your whole career. But they can help grow your catalog, feed listener data, support touring decisions, trigger discovery, and become part of a larger income mix with publishing, merch, live shows, sync, and direct-to-fan revenue. #3: “Music distribution and music publishing are basically the same thing.” The truth: Distribution and publishing deal with two completely different sides of your music. Distribution is what gets your recording onto platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, and more. That’s the master side of the release. Publishing is tied to the song itself: the lyrics, melody, composition, and the people who wrote it. That’s where publishing royalties come in, including performance royalties, mechanical royalties, and other songwriter-side income. This is where artists can easily miss money. Just because your song is live on streaming platforms doesn't mean your publishing is fully handled. You still need to make sure your splits are right, your works are registered, and the right collection systems are in place. Think of it like this: distribution gets the recording out. Publishing helps make sure it's actually earning you money. #4: “If your music is streaming, you’re automatically collecting royalties.” The truth: Getting your music onto streaming platforms is only one part of the royalty collection process. When your song is live, your distributor helps collect the royalties tied to the recording from the platforms they deliver to. But that doesn't automatically cover every royalty your music can earn. If you wrote or co-wrote the song, there may be publishing royalties tied to the composition too. That can include performance royalties, mechanical royalties, and royalties collected through organizations like PROs, The MLC, SoundExchange, and other collection societies, depending on where and how the music is used. If the song is out and the streams are happening, but the right registrations are not in place, those royalties sit unclaimed because the system doesn't have the information needed to get them back to you. To make sure you’re collecting everything you’ve rightfully earned, check out these resources: How Music Royalties Actually Work: Splits, Streaming, and TikTok Payouts Explained How to Track Royalties and Payouts as an Independent Artist The Ultimate Royalties Checklist for Independent Artists #5: “Getting playlisted guarantees streams and success.” The truth: Playlists can help, but they are not a whole release strategy. The right playlist can put your song in front of new listeners, but that doesn’t mean people are actually saving the song, following you, checking out your catalog, or becoming real fans. A spike in streams feels good, sure, but if there’s no follow-through, that momentum will fade once the placement is gone. Use playlisting as one part of the plan. You still need strong content, smart pitching, fan engagement, and a reason for people to care beyond that one song. Want to learn more about playlisting? Check these out: Why Editorial Playlists Aren’t Guaranteed (and What Actually Drives Them) Playlist Pitching 101: How to Tell a Story Editors Actually Care About #6: “An advance is free money!” The truth: An advance is actually an upfront payment against future earnings. An advance can help you pay for recording, marketing, content, touring, or anything else needed to push your release forward. BUT IT IS NOT FREE MONEY. In most deals, the label or partner recoups that advance from your royalties before you start seeing any additional payouts. Don’t let a big number make the decision for you. Look at what income gets recouped, what costs can be added to the balance, how long the term lasts, and what rights you are giving up. A huge advance can look great upfront, but bad terms can cost you more down the line. Check out “Understanding Advances: Everything You Need to Know” to make sure you know what you’re getting yourself into before you sign anything. #7: “If one song blows up, you’ve made it.” The truth: Going viral can get people’s attention, but attention alone doesn’t build a career. Going viral can boost streams, followers, press, playlist interest, or social engagement. That is valuable, but it only lasts if there is something behind it. If people find one song but there is no strong catalog, clear artist identity, live strategy, content plan, or way to keep them engaged, the moment fades fast. Use the attention while you have it. Push people to your other music, capture the audience, tell your story, and give new listeners a reason to stick around after the trend is over. #8: “You have to be famous to make money in music.” The truth: You don’t need millions of followers to build real income from your music. Fame is one version of success, but it’s definitely not the only way to make money. A sustainable music career more commonly comes from multiple income streams working together. Streaming, publishing, sync, merch, live shows, production, fan subscriptions, teaching, brand deals, direct-to-fan sales, and more. You don’t have to be “famous” to the general public to make music your career. If you have a loyal audience that streams your music, buys your merch, shows up to your shows, and so on, that is a real business in itself. Don’t let the idea of fame blind you from the very real opportunities available to you. If you really want to build a sustainable career in music, you can do so with or without a viral moment. #9: “All I have to do is upload my song, and my distributor does the rest.” The truth: Your distributor gets your music delivered, but they are not responsible for your entire release efforts. A distributor helps get your music onto platforms and pays out the royalties they collect from those platforms. But distribution is not the same as having a full team behind your release. You are still responsible for your rollout, metadata, publishing setup, royalty registrations, content, pitching, fan engagement, and what happens after the song goes live. Uploading the song is one step. Building momentum around it is up to you. That said, we offer hundreds of articles for FREE right here on the Symphonic Blog to help you grow your career and stay up to date with the latest trends in the industry. If you want to build a strategy that actually works, check these out: How to Plan a Release Strategy That Spans the Entire Year Why Real Music Marketing is More Than Just Promotion… It’s Strategy How To Use Music Data to Guide Your Next Release as an Independent Artist Best Practices for Maximum Release Potential as a Symphonic Client #10: “If I own my masters, I own all the rights to my song.” The truth: Owning your masters means you own the recording, not every right connected to the song. Your master is the specific sound recording. The composition is the underlying song: the lyrics, melody, and songwriting. Those are separate rights. So yes, owning your masters gives you control over the recording, which is huge. But that does not automatically settle who owns the composition, who gets publishing, or how collaborators get paid. This is why split sheets and clear agreements matter from the beginning. If a producer made the beat, someone helped write the hook, a featured artist added a verse, or there are multiple writers involved, everyone should know their percentage before the song comes out. NOTE: That includes songwriter splits, master royalty splits if applicable, producer points, featured artist terms, publishing shares, and any sample or beat license restrictions. Getting this in writing early makes it easier to register the song correctly, pay everyone properly, and avoid messy disputes once the song starts earning money. #11: “Using a beat I found online is fine as long as I credit the producer.” The truth: Credit is not the same as permission. If you find a beat online and want to use it, you need to understand what rights you actually have. Contrary to popular belief, a producer credit doesn’t automatically give you permission to release the song, monetize it, pitch it for sync, or use it however you want. That all depends on the license. Some beats are exclusive. Some are non-exclusive, which means other artists can use the same beat too. Some licenses allow commercial releases but limit streams, videos, monetization, sync, or other uses. Before you release anything, read the terms and make sure you know what you’re allowed to do with the beat. If the agreement is vague, missing, or hard to understand, clear it up before the song goes live. Crediting the producer is important, but the license is what protects you. Some Final Thoughts… In the age of social media, it’s hard not to compare yourself to everyone else. Every win on the feed, every story of overnight success, it’s easy to let all of that throw off your internal compass and make you question if your path is the right one. But in reality, success in the music industry isn’t one-size-fits-all. There’s no single way to build a career, no perfect timeline, and no shortcut that works for everyone. Your story may feel slower, quieter, or less explosive than your favorite artist, but that doesn’t make it any less real. Building something sustainable takes time. It takes actually learning how things work, and making decisions based on what’s right for YOU, and nobody else. Don’t worry about following someone else's map.
