content: “How do I get my music on Spotify playlists?” is one of the most common questions we get from independent artists at CD Baby. It’s no surprise — popular playlists like Spotify’s official editorials can skyrocket an artist’s streams overnight. But bad actors have also recognized the power these playlists have — and built an entire industry around faking them. These actors create playlists that use bot activity to drive up their streams. This artificial streaming activity can ruin artists’ algorithmic standing and at worst, get their music removed from the platform. In this blog, we’ll run through five ways to avoid Spotify playlists that employ artificial streaming and conclude with a bit of perspective on how playlists should fit within your strategy for growing your fan base. KEY TAKEAWAYS Never pay for guaranteed streams: Legitimate playlist placement is never "bought" — any service promising guaranteed streams or virality for a fee is a red flag for bot activity and playlist scams. Watch your Spotify for Artists data: Sudden streaming spikes, unusual listener locations, or high streams-per-listener ratios can signal your music has been swept into a botted playlist without your knowledge. Vet curator profiles before trusting a playlist: Generic usernames, fake followers, and profiles mimicking official Spotify editorial branding are common signs of an inauthentic playlist. Use Spotify's own tools first: Pitching directly to Spotify editorial playlists, building your own Artist Playlists, and encouraging fans to playlist your music are all safer, more sustainable ways to grow streams than third-party promotion services. Playlists are an acquisition tool, not a growth strategy: Real fan connection (through live shows, email lists, and social media) is key to growing your music career. Playlists help get more ears on your music, but it’s up to you to retain new fans. 1. Use Spotify’s own playlist tools If you have a release coming up, pitch your music to Spotify’s editorial playlists. (Spotify recommends pitching four weeks out or more to maximize your chances of placement.) You can also create your own playlists — mixing your music with your favorite tracks from friends, influences, and comparable artists. Promote these playlists to your fans and add them to your Spotify artist profile as Artist Playlists to boost your streams. Lastly, encourage your fans to create playlists of their own with your music — gamify it by awarding a playlist that best captures your influence or fits a certain theme. 2. Do your research before using a playlist promotion service As a categorical rule, never use a service that guarantees streams in exchange for payment. In general, if a service sounds too good to be true, it isn’t legitimate. Here are some other signs a service is a scam or using botted traffic: No contactable human providing the service No real information about how the service promotes your music or examples of the playlists they use Unrealistic promises like virality or guaranteed streaming counts Cold or unsolicited outreach over emails or social media Requests for a “donation” or “fee” to keep your music on a playlist No signs of verified legitimacy from reputable sources (other artists, online reviews, etc.) 3. Monitor your streaming activity in Spotify for Artists Your music can get swept up in bot traffic without your consent — and you can still be penalized for it. That’s why it’s crucial to stay on top of your streaming data in Spotify for Artists and watch for suspicious activity. A few metrics worth monitoring closely: Top playlists: Treat any unexpected placement on a large playlist with caution. (More on how to evaluate playlist legitimacy in the next section.) Streams over time: An unexpected spike in listenership can signal a new playlist placement or bot activity. Drill down to see where those listeners are actually coming from and take stock of your own promo efforts — have you run ads or played major shows that could account for the spike? Listeners per location: Unexplained spikes in areas you haven’t been promoting are suspicious — particularly any low population areas with disproportionately high streaming numbers. Streams per listener: This can vary naturally — especially for new artists who might be encouraging their same inner circle to listen multiple times — but watch out for suspicious ratios (i.e. anything more than the casual 3-5 times per listener). 4. Investigate the playlists your music appears on Routinely check your top playlist placements in Spotify for Artists to verify the authenticity of the playlists and the curators. You can use this same criteria for checking the legitimacy of playlists that a third-party promo service uses as well, but be aware that even if everything seems to check out, these platforms still carry risks. If you suspect your music has been placed on a botted playlist, report it to Spotify. Here’s what to look out for at the playlist level: Curator profile: Look out for generic profiles with inauthentic profile photos, nonsense usernames, and approximately the same amount of saves on every playlist they own. Curator followers: Real accounts should have mostly real followers. If an account is generic and also has fake followers (nonsense usernames, no profile photos, and no user activity), steer clear. Playlist curation: Be wary of user-generated playlists that mimic the look of official editorial playlists — with a Spotify logo in the top left, the same Spotify font, and lifestyle imagery. They’re trying to mislead you. Also avoid playlists that don’t have any clear curational vision or coherency and a robotic or nonsense description. 5. Focus on real fan connection If you’re an emerging artist, build a solid foundation for your fans before you chase playlist placements. That means claiming and optimizing profiles across streaming and social platforms, planning a well-rounded release strategy, and doubling down on the channels where you connect best with fans — live performances, online forums, email newsletters, and social media. Streams you gain from a strong playlist placement won’t necessarily earn you loyal fans if you don’t have a strong strategy to retain new listeners. Treat playlists as an acquisition tool — not your entire playbook. If you do land on your dream playlist, make it count. When a curious new listener clicks through from the playlist to your profile — then to your social media — that’s your chance to make a strong first impression. That listener is looking to learn more about you, spot shared followers and similar artists, and see that you're active and serious about your music. All of that work lies beyond chasing playlists. The truth: Fan growth is hard work Playlists are attractive for fast and easy streaming growth, but never put your music at risk by employing a predatory service or by taking unexpected spikes in listenership at face value. Follow the tips in this blog to protect your music and focus on building systems to genuinely connect with fans. Building a strong foundation of die-hard fans will always be more valuable than amassing a transient audience through playlisting alone. content: The following post is an op-ed from CD Baby's SVP of Product Sean Hallarman. It originally appeared on the Downtown Music blog. I came back from this year’s Music Biz conference convinced there’s never been a better time to be an independent artist. Panel after panel, demo after demo, I witnessed an explosion of new technologies that didn’t exist just a few years ago. AI – with the right support from a human – that will master your record, generate the artwork, and create a suite of marketing assets. Platforms that offer direct ownership of the fan relationship, rather than reach rented from an algorithm. And the part that stayed with me is that these tools are reaching a bedroom artist and a major label’s marketing team at the same moment. Access has been flattened. That flattening is one of the best things to happen to independent music in years. But it comes with a quieter challenge: when an artist can suddenly do almost anything, where do they start? Imagine finishing your first recording and getting ready to release it to the world. All the years you spent getting to that moment focused on creating art, and now you’re ready to introduce it into culture. At face value, it may seem that releasing that music is as simple as posting to social media. But the moment you distribute, you’ve suddenly opened a business: rights to sort out, royalty splits to agree, marketing campaigns to plan, streaming data to analyze. You’re confronted with decisions that’ll have long-term effects that are hard to undo once set in place. And now, on top of all that, there’s a wall of platforms and tools, each more powerful than the one that preceded it. Any one of them might help, which is exactly what makes it so hard to know what to reach for first. That navigation problem is the part I keep coming back to, because as the entry point for independent artists to distribute their music, it’s increasingly our responsibility to solve. Even if it might make short-term commercial sense to bundle every capability an artist might eventually need into a single offering upfront, it doesn’t always serve artists. The better approach is to help them identify the right tool for the right moment in their development. Early on, it almost always comes down to the same thing: building connections with fans. The right tools make that easier. Analytics that show where a song is starting to resonate. Advertising that widens a circle already leaning in. Direct-to-fan tools that deepen the relationships worth keeping. But which of those actually fits at this stage depends on the artist. Some will love the data deep-dives, and others never will. Some come alive running a small, devoted community on a niche platform, and others don’t. That’s not a problem to solve. It’s just who they are. Connection only works when it’s authentic to the artist making it. The right tools don’t ask every artist to become the same kind of entrepreneur; they help each one lean into their own strengths at the right stage of their career. This is where music companies serving independent artists should act as guides, not just vendors. We’ve been thinking deeply about the standard we need to set for ourselves in serving DIY artists. The most exciting thing about this moment is not just that independent artists can now do most things a major label can do; it’s that they have more freedom than ever to decide what kind of career they want to build. We believe the measure of a useful platform is as much about helping them get their music heard as it is about helping them understand what matters now, what can wait, and what choices will protect their interests over the long term. It’s no longer enough to offer independent artists a bigger toolbox. We need to better serve them as a guide. content: Choosing your release date is about more than finding an open day on the calendar. Being strategic about timing can significantly boost your streams and help your release reach its full potential. The right date depends on several factors — from giving yourself and your fans enough lead time, to matching the sound and message of your music with the right moment. In this blog, we'll walk through the key considerations to help you land on the right date. KEY TAKEAWAYS Set your release date at least four weeks to prepare promo materials, platform profiles, and engage fans Fridays are the industry-standard release day, but earlier weekdays can help you stand out from the crowd Tying your release to a live show or other tentpole moment can drive early streams Consider holiday deadlines, eligibility windows, and press roundup timing Maintaining a consistent release cadence can help sustain momentum over time 1. Be proactive Set your release date at least four weeks in the future. That gives you time to gather promotional material, claim and set up platform profiles, and engage your fans. Ideally, choose your release date before or during the recording process to ensure you’re not scrambling to finalize details when you submit your music for distribution. 2. Release on Friday or go your own way From Spotify’s Release Radar (which refreshes every Friday morning) to press and blog Friday roundups, the music industry is built around Friday release days. Over 60 percent of releases CD Baby distributed in 2025 fell on a Friday. But independent artists have also seen success skipping the crowds on Friday to release in the earlier, quieter days of the week. Decide what’s best for you — but generally weekends get a bit lost in the mix. The next tip might help you narrow down your date further. 3. Line up your release date with a show or other tentpole moment Do you have an upcoming opening slot for a touring act, a release show booked, or a party planned? Consider setting your release date on a day that your fans will be engaged — that helps lock in some early streams and lets release day feel like the celebration you deserve. You can book a release show at a local venue, then set your release date for that day. 4. Be mindful of the time of year – holidays, seasons, cultural moments, deadlines, and more Releasing music at the right moment can amplify its impact, while poor timing can just as easily hold it back. Know your sound and how to describe it, then decide where it fits into the broader calendar. A love (or anti-love) song might do well around Valentine’s Day, a beachy, high-energy track might be best received in the summer, or a gloomy, weepy track might do best in colder months. Showing this intentionality in your releases makes them easier to market and more likely that your fans will listen. Ultimately, how you decide to leverage holidays, seasons, cultural moments and more is completely subjective. But here a few important deadlines to consider: GRAMMY Awards: If you’re interested in pursuing a GRAMMY nomination, ensure your release falls within the eligibility period. In 2026, that’s between August 31, 2025 and August 28, 2026. Distributor Holiday Deadlines: If you’re looking to release a holiday track (anywhere from November to early January), follow your distributor’s holiday deadline schedule. If you’re a CD Baby artist, keep an eye out for our 2026 deadlines, which we’ll announce in October. Industry Press Roundups: If you’re looking to be considered for industry press roundups (best of the week, month, year), it’s generally best practice to release music before editors are finalizing those lists. For a week, avoid Saturday and Sunday releases, for the month, avoid releasing on the final days of the month, and for the year, try to release by late November. These are of course, not hard and fast rules, but general guidance. 5. Find a release cadence that fits your audience Every artist’s fanbase is different, but having a release cadence (a standard amount of time between each release) can help keep your fans engaged. If you’re working your way up to an album, releasing singles every four to six weeks can help build momentum ahead of the full drop. You can use the waterfall release strategy to compound those streams, re-releasing previous singles with new tracks to gain incremental momentum, instead of just dropping the whole album in one go. Check out our recaps of two cornerstone reports from 2025 — Luminate and IFPI’s Global Music Report — to get a confident grasp of topline industry stats and trends. 1. Fans are streaming more music than ever before Global on-demand audio streams hit 2.8 trillion in the first half of 2026, up 9.8% from the 2.5 trillion streams in the same period last year. What this means: Release your music to find your audience. Record-breaking streaming volume means more opportunities to build your fanbase. 2. Independent music distribution continues to grow Independently distributed tracks have grown across the mid- and lower-volume streaming tiers, demonstrating how independent sectors are carving out a sustainable ecosystem outside the mainstream. What this means: You don’t need a viral hit to lead a successful independent career. Focus on finding your niche audience, honing your brand as an artist, and leveraging the increasing array of marketing tools and services available to independent artists. 3. R&B/hip-hop declines slightly, while dance/electronic grows R&B/hip-hop slightly declined this year, losing a 1.6 share of points year-over-year. But make no mistake, the genre still dominates U.S. streams, accounting for about one in every four streams. Meanwhile, the dance/electronic genre saw the most growth (+18.9% year-over-year on-demand audio change). What this means: You can take shifts in genre listenership as encouragement to experiment with your sound, but don’t chase the trends or lose sight of your own artistic identity. 4. CD sales outpaced vinyl, but there’s more to the story CD sales grew 16%, outpacing vinyl sales that grew by a modest 2.4%. K-pop fans account for a significant share of this growth. So much so that excluding sales from BTS’ latest album ARIRANG and other K-pop sales, U.S. CD sales would have been up only 6.7% in the first half of 2026. But interestingly, only half of the Gen Z and Millennial CD buyers actually own a CD player, signalling the act of buying physical music is about aesthetic ownership and providing financial support to an artist as it is listening to the music on the medium itself. What this means: Don’t write off physical formats — or collectibles in general. Whether it’s actual physical releases (CDs, tapes, and vinyl) or standard merch items like shirts and stickers — give your fans a way to support you. 5. Rock music exemplifies the power of catalog music 75% of rock listening comes from tracks older than 60 months — what Luminate calls “deep catalog” listening. That’s in contrast to a genre like world music, where 34% of streams come from “current” tracks (0-18) months and another 26.5% come from tracks that are five years old or newer. What this means: No matter your genre, rock music proves you shouldn’t neglect your back catalog. Promote older tracks with the momentum you gain from new releases (e.g. “if you like the new track, listen to this one) and consider strategic re-releases and anniversary campaigns. content: “I don’t want to give up all the juice,” Michael Mwenso says, “but listen: the real key is you take all that stuff that you say is old, you mix it up, and then you get something new.” The belief that “nothing is old if you haven’t heard it before” is somewhat of a guiding principle for Michael. This month, we sat down with the artist, creator, curator, and educator to discuss his new single “Be Free,” his creative process, and advice he has for emerging artists. You can watch the full interview below or read on for key takeaways. About Mwenso Born in West Africa, Michael moved to London with his mother as a child. When his mother was deported to Nigeria, he found solace in Black music — listening to records, spending countless nights at Ronnie Scott’s Jazz Club, and eventually finding mentorship in great artists like James Brown. That early foundation set the direction for everything that followed. Wynton Marsalis invited him to join the programming team as curator at Jazz at Lincoln Center. There, he developed late night programming at Dizzy’s Club and networked with new musicians to start his group, Mwenso & The Shakes. With his creative collaborator, Jono Gasparro, he later co-founded Electric Root, which partners with institutions to decolonize music curricula with anti-racist, artist-led programming. And in 2022, he won an Emmy for Michael Mwenso Honors George Floyd, a documentary special that demonstrated his deeply held belief that art and activism are one. Mwenso’s new single, “Be Free” After more than a decade in the United States, Michael recently returned to London, and released his solo debut single “Be Free” — the first track off his upcoming album. Where much of his work to date has centered on collective language, the new single captures Michael taking on a more personal lyrical perspective and pushing his vocals to new heights. The single's release lined up with the Jon Batiste World Festival, a multi-night residency at Koko in London that Michael co-curated with Batiste. It was the perfect, organic platform for promoting “Be Free.” 3 lessons for independent artists from Mwenso Michael opened up about the people, values, and musical ideas that keep him inspired. The following three pieces of advice from our conversation stood out — lightly edited for brevity. 1. Love the music, but love the people first Michael has spent most of his life creating spaces, platforms, and events for artists to perform and connect with people. The secret to his success in curation? Loving people. He explained that every performance provides an opportunity for listeners to reconnect with the artists, experiences, and emotions that shape a musical lineage. Enabling that as a curator is a selfless and spiritual exercise, Michael notes, and a source of true joy. 2. Embody the qualities of successful artists Asked what it takes to succeed today, Michael pointed to three successful artists, each of whom exemplify characteristics he values: James Brown demonstrated focus and concentration, Wynton Marsalis showcases discipline, consistency, and practice, and Jon Batiste exemplifies foresight, calculation, and manifestation. 3. Nothing is old if you haven’t heard it yet Michael believes futuristic music comes from keeping the past alive and reinterpreting it. "Just because it's from nineteen-something doesn't mean you can't play it with fire and funk now," he said. In his framework, tradition pushes music forward, instead of holding it in place. What will you take from Mwenso’s story? Here are a few actionable tips based on what he shared: Build creative spaces (or support those who do) in your community for rehearsal, performance, networking, and inspiration Learn from your heroes — identify the characteristics that propelled their careers and seek to embody those in your work Break free of the shallowness of trends and the stuffiness of tradition – trace your inspirations back to their origins and aim to create something new from what you find Join over 2 million artists, like Mwenso Ready to make your statement?
